label: Reference aid; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern.

sections.title: Grounded conductors — how they are identified
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 200 is about the grounded conductor, which in a house is usually the neutral. Its job in this article is identification: how a worker can tell, by color, marking, or terminal, which conductor is grounded so nobody lands it in the wrong place. It does not size the neutral — that work lives in Articles 210, 215, 220, and 250.
The working rules:
• Smaller insulated grounded conductors carry a continuous white or gray outer finish, or white or gray with colored stripes other than green (200.6)
• Larger grounded conductors may use that same finish, or be identified at their terminations and at accessible points in the ways the section allows (200.6)
• White or gray is reserved for the grounded conductor. The narrow exceptions — a re-identified conductor in a cable assembly used as a hot for a switch loop or a 240V circuit, and flexible cord uses — require the re-identification to be permanent and visible where required (200.7)
• A white conductor is never an equipment ground. Equipment grounds are green, green with yellow stripes, or bare (200.7)
sections.on_the_job: Treat white and gray as a warning label, not a suggestion. Before you splice, land, or re-mark a conductor, check what it is actually connected to at both ends. In a feeder panel fed from a Sharma meter-main, the picture in the drawing is the standard: white neutrals on the isolated neutral bar, green and bare grounds on their own bar, black hots on breakers. Where the white of a cable assembly is re-identified as the hot of a switch loop, tape it a hot color at every box it appears in, so the next worker is not guessing.
sections.figure_idea: A panel detail showing a white insulated neutral landed on the isolated neutral bar, a green ground on the ground bar, and a black hot on a breaker, each labeled.
sections.why_it_exists: A neutral landed in the wrong place is not a paperwork error. Land a hot where a neutral belongs and metal parts sit energized; swap neutral and ground and current rides the grounding system full-time. Color and terminal identification is the one check every worker can make at a glance, in every box, without a meter — which is why the Code guards the white and gray so strictly.
inspection_fails: White conductor used as a switch-loop hot with no re-identification marking in the switch box or the fixture box.
Large feeder neutral landed with no identification at its terminations.
White or gray conductor used as an equipment grounding conductor.
Re-identified white marked at one end only; the far end still reads as a neutral.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer gives Article 200 a job it does not have: 'size the neutral under 200.6.' Identification lives here; sizing lives in Articles 210, 215, 220 and 250. Second trap: 'a white wire can be taped green and used as the equipment ground.' Never — white or gray is reserved for the grounded conductor, and grounds are green, green with yellow stripes, or bare.

rows: White or gray finish; larger sizes may be marked at terminations (200.6)
Green, green with yellow stripes, or bare

figures.alt: Panel detail with white grounded conductors landed on an isolated neutral bar, green and bare equipment grounds on a ground bar, a black hot on a breaker, and a white conductor re-identified with black tape.

page_quiz.question: Article 200 covers which job?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Article 200 is identification only — color, marking and terminals. Sizing lives in Articles 210, 215, 220 and 250.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 200.7 allows the re-identified conductor in a cable assembly, permanently marked and visible where required.

sections.title: The neutral serves its own circuit
sections.plain_explanation: A grounded (neutral) conductor belongs to the circuit it was run with. It may not be borrowed to carry return current for a different circuit, and a neutral from one circuit or system may not be shared with another unless the arrangement is one the Code specifically builds — the multiwire branch circuit being the common one in a house. Where a neutral is shared, every rule for that shared arrangement (same raceway or cable, grouped disconnecting means, identification) has to be followed end to end. A neutral picked up from a nearby box because it was handy is a violation and a shock hazard: switching off one breaker leaves the shared neutral still carrying the other circuit's current.
sections.on_the_job: Troubleshooting rule: if you open a box and find a neutral spliced to a circuit it did not arrive with, stop and trace both ends before you land anything. On a multiwire circuit, killing one breaker does not make the neutral safe — that is why the two hots disconnect together (see the 210.4 page).
sections.figure_idea: Two circuits at one panel: one with its own neutral run beside it (correct), one borrowing a neutral from the circuit next door (crossed out).

nec2023_change.change: No new rule here. The one-neutral-per-circuit limit stands, and a new note points you to 215.4, the place where feeders can share a common neutral. New informational note: for feeders that share one neutral, look to 215.4 for the allowance.

sections.why_it_exists: A neutral carries the return current of its own circuit, and everything downstream assumes that is true — the breaker, the GFCI and AFCI sensing, and the next man who opens a box. Borrow a neutral from the circuit next door and one breaker can be off while that neutral still carries the other circuit's load: a shock waiting inside a 'dead' box. A borrowed neutral also returns current along a path nobody planned, and a loose one overheats quietly inside a wall.
inspection_fails: Neutral for one circuit borrowed from a different circuit in the same box.
Shared neutral whose ungrounded conductors do not disconnect together — one breaker off, neutral still carrying load.
Multiwire circuit hots landed on the same leg, so the neutral carries the sum of both loads.
Neutrals from two circuits spliced together in a junction box downstream of the panel.
sections.exam_trap: Trap one: 'turning off one breaker makes a shared neutral safe.' It does not — the other circuit is still returning through it. Trap two: 'a feeder may never share a neutral.' It may, under 215.4 — the 2023 note points there. What is never allowed is borrowing a neutral the Code did not build for sharing.

sections.title: How a grounded conductor is marked
sections.plain_explanation:
This section gives the ways a grounded conductor — usually the neutral — may be identified, and the method changes with conductor size.
• 6 AWG or smaller: a continuous white or gray outer finish, or three continuous white or gray stripes on insulation other than green, along the entire length. The identification is the insulation itself, from the factory — white tape wrapped at the ends of a small black conductor does not meet the rule.
• Larger than 6 AWG: the same finishes, or — at the time of installation — a distinctive white or gray marking that encircles the conductor at its terminations.
Only the grounded conductor is identified this way; white and gray are reserved for it. See 200.7 for the narrow cases where a white conductor in a cable assembly may be re-identified as a hot.
sections.on_the_job: On rough-in, pick the right roll — do not plan to tape your way out of the wrong insulation color on small branch wiring. The 12 AWG neutrals in a house come off a white roll, period. On larger feeders, mark every accessible point, not just the end you happen to be landing today: the black feeder neutral in a Siemens subpanel may be identified with white tape that fully encircles it at the panel, at the disconnect, and at every point where the conductor is accessible.
sections.figure_idea: Three feeder conductors at a panel: black, red, and one wrapped with white tape at the end, with a note that small branch conductors use factory white or gray insulation.
sections.why_it_exists: Everyone who opens a box trusts the colors. A neutral that looks like a hot gets landed on a breaker or spliced into the wrong circuit, and the next person who trusts the marking grabs a conductor that is live when it should not be. Identification that runs the full length on small conductors — and that completely encircles the conductor where termination marking is allowed — is what makes that trust safe.
inspection_fails: Black 12 AWG landed as a neutral with white tape on the ends. At 6 AWG or smaller the finish itself must be white or gray.
Feeder neutral taped at the panel but left unmarked at the disconnect — the termination marking is missing at one end.
Tape applied as a flag that does not encircle the conductor. 200.6(B) marking must encircle it.
White stripes relied on over green insulation. The stripe option is for insulation other than green.
A white conductor landed on a breaker with no re-identification marking (see 200.7).
sections.exam_trap: The trap: a black 8 AWG conductor with white tape at both ends, offered as the neutral. It fails — 8 AWG is in the 6 AWG-or-smaller class, where the finish itself must be white or gray. The same tape job on a 1/0 feeder conductor is exactly what 200.6(B) permits. The size, not the tape, decides.

The same finishes, or a white or gray marking encircling the conductor at its terminations, applied at installation
tables.note: Termination marking is not an option at 6 AWG or smaller.

figures.alt: Two conductor examples: at 6 AWG or smaller a white-insulated conductor passes and a black conductor with tape at the ends fails; larger than 6 AWG a black feeder conductor with white tape encircling it at its terminations passes; a size scale marks the break point at 6 AWG.

sections.title: What white or gray insulation may be used for
sections.plain_explanation:
White or gray insulation is reserved for the grounded conductor, with narrow exceptions the section spells out. The color is a promise, and for circuits of 50 volts or more the promise may be bent only in these ways (200.7(C)):
• Cable assemblies. A white conductor inside a cable assembly may serve as a hot — the familiar field examples are a re-identified conductor in a cable assembly used as a hot for a switch loop or a 240V circuit, and the marking has to be permanent: re-identified at its termination and at every location where it is visible and accessible, with the marking encircling the insulation in a color other than white, gray or green.
• Switch loops. The re-identified white may supply the switch, or run as a traveler between 3-way and 4-way switches. It may not be the return conductor from the switch back to the outlet.
• Flexible cords. A white conductor in a flexible cord may be used as a hot only where the cord rules permit it (400.7).
In a raceway there is no re-identification at all — individual conductors are pulled in the right color. And a white conductor is never free to be a ground; equipment grounds are green, green with yellow stripes, or bare.
sections.on_the_job: If you re-identify a white wire as a hot, mark it at every box where it appears and tell the trim crew. If you open a box and find an unmarked white on a switch or breaker, stop and trace it instead of assuming. The everyday Sharma case is the 240 V water heater wired in a two-wire cable assembly: the white is re-identified with black tape that encircles it, at the heater and again at the breaker. Mark one end only and the job is half done — the other end is where the next person gets surprised.
sections.sharma_note: Never backstab and never guess a re-identified white — Sharma crews trace it. See S-10 for conductor and termination practice generally.
sections.why_it_exists: The next person to open the box trusts the color before anything else. A white wire that is secretly a hot shocks the person who treats it as a neutral; a white wire used as a ground leaves equipment looking grounded when it is not. Reserving the color — and marking every exception so it cannot be missed — is what makes that trust safe.
sections.exam_trap: The exam's favorite wrong answers: 'a white conductor may be re-identified anywhere if it is taped' — no, the allowance covers cable assemblies and flexible cords, never individual conductors in a raceway. And 'the re-identified white in a switch loop can carry the switched return back to the light' — no, it may only supply the switch, or run as a traveler; the return is a colored conductor.
inspection_fails: White conductor landed on a breaker with no re-identification marking anywhere.
Re-identified white marked at the panel but not at the far box where it is visible and accessible.
White conductor used as the equipment grounding conductor on a retrofit.
White THHN pulled in conduit and taped black to serve as a hot.

The return from a switch back to the outlet, in a switch loop
No — supply to the switch only
A hot in a raceway, taped at the ends
tables.note: Re-identification must encircle the insulation and be a color other than white, gray or green.

figures.caption: White is the grounded color: one OK use, two common violations.

page_quiz.question: A white conductor in a cable assembly may be used as a hot when it is:

page_quiz.explain_plain: The marking must encircle the insulation, in a color other than white, gray or green, everywhere the conductor can be seen.

sections.title: Terminal identification and polarity
sections.plain_explanation: Terminals tell you where the grounded conductor lands. On receptacles, switches, lampholders and other devices, the terminal for the grounded conductor is identified — a silver-colored screw, or a terminal marked with the word WHITE — while the ungrounded (hot) terminal is brass or dark colored, and the equipment-grounding terminal is green. That green-terminal rule is 250.126, not Article 200. Polarity is the matching rule in 200.11: the grounded conductor goes to the identified terminal, never reversed. On a standard receptacle that puts the neutral on the longer slot and the hot on the shorter one, so a plug's wide blade lands on the neutral side. The screw shell of a lampholder is the grounded-conductor terminal (200.10(C)).
sections.on_the_job: Reversed polarity is one of the most common findings in older Florida houses: the receptacle works, but the tester shows the fault. Land white on silver, black on brass, green on green, and check with a polarity tester at final — a lamp lighting up proves nothing about polarity. On a Kissimmee rewire, six receptacles on one circuit tested reversed because the first device was landed white-on-brass and every downstream device copied it. Twenty minutes with a tester at trim-out caught what the rough-in missed.
sections.figure_idea: Duplex receptacle from the back: silver screw with the white conductor, brass screw with the black, green screw with the ground, and the face slots labeled to match.
sections.why_it_exists: Polarity decides which parts of a device sit at line voltage when it is off or unplugged. A lamp with a reversed lampholder leaves its screw shell hot with the switch off, and a reversed receptacle puts voltage on the side of the plug a person expects to be safe. Identified terminals make the safe connection the obvious one.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the receptacle works, so it is wired right.' A reversed receptacle runs a lamp or a drill perfectly — the fault only shows on a tester. Second trap: the longer slot is the neutral. Picking the longer slot as the hot reverses every plug-in load on the circuit.
inspection_fails: White conductor landed on the brass terminal — reversed polarity at the receptacle.
Lampholder screw shell connected to the hot conductor. The shell is the grounded-conductor terminal, 200.10(C).
Ground wire landed on the silver terminal. Silver is for the grounded (neutral) conductor; the equipment ground goes on the green terminal.
Receptacle replaced without checking polarity — the tester shows hot/neutral reversed at final.

tables.caption: Terminal identification at a glance
tables.note: Face check: the longer slot is the neutral side; the shorter slot is the hot.

figures.alt: Back view of a duplex receptacle: silver screws on the left for the white grounded conductor, brass screws on the right for the black hot conductor, and a green screw at the bottom for the equipment ground; below, the face with the longer neutral slot and the shorter hot slot.
figures.caption: Land by color on the back; the face agrees.

page_quiz.question: On a lampholder, the grounded conductor connects to:

sections.title: Branch circuits — the circuits that feed the load
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 210 governs the final run of wiring that delivers power to lights, receptacles, and appliances — the branch circuits. It sets circuit ratings, the protection people need from shock and arc faults, which dedicated circuits a dwelling must have, where receptacles and lights must go, and how much load a circuit may carry. Most of Sharma's rough-in and trim work is judged against this article.
The article in working order:
• Ratings and loads: what a branch circuit may feed and how it is protected
• Protection: GFCI in 210.8 and AFCI in 210.12, where each applies
• Required dwelling circuits: the named small-appliance, laundry, bathroom and garage circuits of 210.11(C)
• Receptacle placement: the spacing and location rules of 210.52
• Lighting outlets: the switched outlets of 210.70
What Article 210 does not do: it does not identify the grounded conductor (Article 200), size feeders (Article 215), calculate loads (Article 220) or size the service (Article 230).
sections.on_the_job: Read a house plan through Article 210 first: protection, dedicated circuits, receptacle layout, then lighting outlets. That order catches the expensive misses before wire is pulled. On the Marion Oaks spec houses that means walking the plan once for 210.8 and 210.12 protection, once for the 210.11(C) named circuits — two small-appliance, laundry, bathroom, garage — once for 210.52 spacing, and once for 210.70 lighting outlets. On commercial work, remember S-01: Sharma runs 20A minimum branch circuits, stricter than this article requires for dwellings.
sections.sharma_note: S-01: on commercial work Sharma runs 20A minimum branch circuits — stricter than this article requires for dwellings.
sections.figure_idea: A house floor plan with circuits color-coded: kitchen small-appliance, laundry, bathroom, garage, and general area circuits each in a different color.

sections.why_it_exists: Branch circuits are the part of the system people touch every day — every receptacle, switch and light in the building hangs off one. Undersized, overloaded or unprotected branch circuits are where shocks, nuisance trips and electrical fires start, so this article carries the protection and layout rules the inspector checks room by room.

It does — in the 2023 book. Under NEC 2020 the multioutlet ratings are 15, 20, 30, 40 and 50 amps. Check the permit's edition before you reach for a new rule.

sections.title: Multiwire branch circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
A multiwire branch circuit shares one grounded conductor (neutral) between two or three ungrounded conductors taken from different phases or legs. The rules that make it safe:
• Same origin: all conductors of the circuit begin in the same panelboard or similar distribution equipment (210.4(A))
• The shared neutral carries only the unbalanced current. With the hots on opposite legs the currents cancel — two 16 A loads can leave the neutral at 0 A
• Simultaneous disconnect: a means at the panel must open all the hots together — a two-pole breaker or handle-tied breakers (210.4(B))
• Line-to-neutral loads only (210.4(C))
• Grouping: the hots and their shared neutral are grouped together in the panel so the set can be identified (210.4(D))
Land both hots on the same leg and the math flips: the neutral now carries the sum of both loads, on a conductor with no breaker of its own.
sections.on_the_job: Before you share a neutral, prove the breakers are on opposite legs — do not trust position. Adjacent spaces are not opposite legs in every panel layout, and tandem breakers make it worse: two tandems can put both hots on the same leg while looking like a pair. Meter it on the 120/240 V system: 240 V between the two hots means opposite legs; 0 V means the same leg, and the neutral will carry the sum. Use a two-pole breaker, or handle-tied singles, so both hots open together — and on a dual-function job, a two-pole device reads the shared neutral correctly instead of nuisance-tripping on it.
sections.figure_idea: A two-pole breaker feeding a red hot, a black hot, and one shared white neutral to two receptacle runs, with the opposite-leg point circled.

nec2023_change.change: The same-origin rule for multiwire branch circuits now points to 300.3(B)(4), which covers column-width panelboards whose neutrals land in an attached pull box. Hots and neutral of any multiwire branch circuit still begin in one panelboard or other distribution equipment.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.4 Multiwire branch circuits

sections.why_it_exists: The neutral has no overcurrent device watching it. Landed on the same leg, it can carry double current and cook its insulation inside a wall while both breakers sit happy at half load. The second hazard is quieter: open a shared neutral on a live circuit and the two loads end up in series across 240 V — the lighter load can see most of that voltage and burn up.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'Two 20 A multiwire circuits share a neutral, so the neutral must be rated for 40 A.' Wrong — on opposite legs the neutral carries only the difference between the loads, never more than the larger one. The 40 A answer describes the wiring error, not the rule: land both hots on one leg and the neutral really does carry the sum, with nothing there to trip.
inspection_fails: Both hots of a multiwire circuit landed on the same leg — neutral found overheated, insulation brittle, and no breaker ever tripped.
Two single-pole breakers with no handle tie: one circuit worked on live while the shared neutral still carried the other circuit's current.
Multiwire conductors not grouped in the panel — the shared neutral landed with the wrong pair of hots.
Shared neutral spliced through a receptacle instead of pigtailed, so removing the device opens the neutral on a live circuit.

figures.alt: Comparison diagram of a multiwire branch circuit: landed on opposite legs the shared neutral carries 0 A with two 16 A loads; landed on the same leg it carries 32 A and overheats with no breaker tripping.
figures.caption: Opposite legs, the neutral rests. Same leg, it carries both loads.

page_quiz.question: Two multiwire loads draw 16 A each on opposite legs. What does the shared neutral carry?
page_quiz.explain_plain: On opposite legs the currents cancel; the neutral carries only the unbalanced (difference) current.

page_quiz.question: What disconnecting means does a multiwire branch circuit need at the panel?
choices: Each hot on its own single-pole breaker, no tie
A means that opens all the hots simultaneously
A fused switch in the neutral
page_quiz.explain_plain: 210.4(B): all ungrounded conductors of the circuit must open together at the point of origin.

page_quiz.question: Why are a multiwire circuit's conductors grouped in the panelboard?
choices: So the shared set can be identified
page_quiz.explain_plain: 210.4(D) requires grouping so the hots and their shared neutral can be identified as one circuit.

sections.title: Identifying branch circuits — colors and directories
sections.plain_explanation: Branch circuits have to be identifiable where they are worked on. Where a building is fed by more than one nominal voltage system — a light-commercial building with both 208Y/120 and 480Y/277 is the common case — the ungrounded conductors of each system are identified by phase and by system, and the identification method has to be posted at each panelboard (or the conductors durably identified by another approved method an inspector can read). The trade color conventions are black, red, blue for 120/208V systems and brown, orange, yellow for 277/480V systems. In a house the same discipline shows up as an accurate panel directory: every breaker labeled for the load it actually serves. The panel-directory rule is 408.4(A) (every circuit and modification legibly identified as to its clear, evident and specific purpose), not 210.5. 210.5(C)(1) applies only where branch circuits are supplied from more than one nominal voltage system, and the identification method must be readily available or permanently posted at each branch-circuit panelboard. The color schemes (black/red/blue, brown/orange/yellow) are trade convention; the NEC does not mandate particular colors for ungrounded conductors.
sections.on_the_job: Write the directory as you trim the panel, not from memory at final. On a two-system commercial job, land the colors to the posted code from the first pull — re-identifying a pulled circuit with tape at every box is slower and gets missed.
sections.figure_idea: Panelboard door with the posted color-code card: two voltage systems, their phase colors, and a directory filled in circuit by circuit.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Identification is what keeps the next person safe and the job fast. In a two-system building, a brown conductor and a black conductor look the same in a dark ceiling until somebody meters them — land 277 V on a 120 V load, or open the wrong system's neutral, and people and equipment get hurt. A posted color code and an honest directory mean the identification survives the crew that pulled the wire.
inspection_fails: Two voltage systems in one building and no identification method posted at the panelboard (210.5(C)(1)).
Ungrounded conductors not identified by phase and by system where more than one nominal voltage system supplies the building.
Panel directory blank, or entries like 'lights' and 'plugs' that do not name a clear, specific purpose (408.4(A)).
Circuits re-identified with tape at some boxes and missed at others, so the posted code cannot be trusted.
sections.exam_trap: Two trap answers live on this page. First: '210.5 requires black, red, blue and brown, orange, yellow.' It does not — those colors are trade convention; 210.5(C)(1) requires identification by phase and by system, with the method posted at each panelboard. Second: citing 210.5 for a missing panel directory. The directory rule is 408.4(A).

tables.caption: Trade color convention — know it, and know it is convention
tables.note: The NEC requires identification by phase and system, with the method posted at each panelboard (210.5(C)(1)); it does not mandate these particular colors.

figures.alt: Panelboard door with the posted identification card for two voltage systems, 208Y/120 with black red blue phase colors and 480Y/277 with brown orange yellow, above a circuit directory filled in circuit by circuit with specific purposes.
figures.caption: The posted card and the directory: identification the next crew can read.

page_quiz.question: A building is supplied by both 208Y/120 and 480Y/277 systems. What does 210.5(C)(1) require?
choices: Ungrounded conductors identified by phase and system, with the method posted at each panelboard
Only black, red and blue conductors anywhere in the building
A label on the meter only
Nothing — the rule is for houses only
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where branch circuits are supplied from more than one nominal voltage system, the ungrounded conductors are identified by phase and by system, and the method is posted at each branch-circuit panelboard.

page_quiz.question: The rule that every circuit in a panelboard directory be legibly identified by its clear, specific purpose is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: The panel-directory rule is 408.4(A), not 210.5 — 210.5 is about identifying conductors by phase and system.

page_quiz.question: Brown, orange and yellow is the trade convention for which system?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Brown, orange, yellow is the trade convention for 277/480 V systems; black, red, blue is the convention for 120/208 V. The NEC requires identification, not these colors.

sections.title: Ground-fault protection for people
sections.plain_explanation:
This section requires ground-fault protection for people in the places where a person, water, concrete or the outdoors make a fault to ground most dangerous. A GFCI watches the current leaving on the hot and returning on the neutral; when they differ, current is leaking through a person or a wet path, and the device opens the circuit. Protection can be provided at the receptacle, at the breaker, or by a device feeding through to downstream outlets, as long as the outlet that needs protection actually gets it — and the device must be readily accessible, not buried behind a refrigerator or dishwasher. The section is organized by where the outlet sits:
• (A) Dwelling units — the location list on the next page
• (B) Other than dwelling units — the commercial and similar locations
• (D) and (F) — specific equipment pages, including dishwashers and outdoor HVAC outlets
The 2020 rule reaches further than older editions: it runs to 250-volt receptacles, so a 240-volt dryer outlet counts, not just the 120-volt points.
sections.on_the_job: Walk a Marion Oaks slab home the way the inspector will: location by location, not room name by room name. The bathroom receptacle, the kitchen countertop receptacles, the receptacle within 6 ft of the laundry sink, the washer outlet and the 240 V dryer outlet, every garage receptacle, and the lanai and soffit outlets all need protection. A receptacle in an unfinished part of a basement, within reach of a sink, or in a laundry area is judged by where it sits, not by what the plan calls the room. Sharma protects at the breaker (S-07): the dual-function breaker carries the protection and the wall device is a standard tamper-resistant receptacle, so test at the breaker and mark the schedule.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: Sharma protects 120V circuits at the breaker with dual-function breakers and installs standard tamper-resistant receptacles at points marked GFI. No GFCI receptacles.
sections.figure_idea: A house diagram with the GFCI locations shaded: bathroom, garage, outdoors, basement, kitchen, sink areas, laundry, and tub/shower areas.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the FBC 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. A local AHJ amendment controls over any general summary here.
sections.why_it_exists: An overload breaker protects wire, not people: it needs many amperes to trip, while a current far below one ampere through a chest can stop a heart. Wet skin, a concrete slab and a grounded faucet lower the body's resistance, so a fault that would be a tingle in a dry bedroom turns lethal at a sink, a tub or a garage floor. The GFCI fills that gap: a Class A device trips at 6 mA or more, long before the current through a person becomes fatal.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering by room name: 'that receptacle is in a storage room, so no GFCI.' Wrong — a receptacle within 6 ft of a laundry sink needs protection whatever the plan calls the room: the list follows the location and the sink, not the label. Second trap: protecting the first receptacle on a run and assuming the rest are covered, when the feed-through device was landed line-to-line and downstream outlets get nothing.
inspection_fails: Receptacle within 6 ft of a sink or tub with no GFCI protection, because the plan labeled the room 'storage'.
Feed-through GFCI landed line-to-line, so the downstream receptacles it was meant to protect test dead to a GFCI tester.
GFCI device hidden behind the refrigerator or the dishwasher, where it is not readily accessible.
240 V dryer receptacle in the laundry area on a standard 2-pole breaker — the 2020 rule covers 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles.
Outdoor receptacle on the lanai or under the soffit left unprotected.

page_quiz.question: A receptacle sits 5 ft from a laundry sink in a room the plan labels 'storage.' GFCI protection required under NEC 2020?
choices: No — storage rooms are not on the list
Yes — the location and the sink decide, not the room name
Only if the floor is concrete
Only when the circuit is 20 A
page_quiz.explain_plain: 210.8 follows where the receptacle sits. Within 6 ft of a sink bowl — and in a laundry area — protection is required whatever the room is called.

page_quiz.question: Sharma's standard way to protect a whole 120 V circuit under S-07 is:
choices: A GFCI receptacle at the last outlet
A dual-function breaker in the panel
A GFCI receptacle at every outlet
A feed-through device in the attic
page_quiz.explain_plain: S-07 puts the protection at the breaker with dual-function breakers; the wall devices are standard tamper-resistant receptacles.

page_quiz.question: A Class A GFCI opens the circuit when the difference between outgoing and returning current reaches about:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Class A ground-fault protection trips at 6 mA or more — far below what an overload breaker sees, and below a lethal current through a person.

sections.title: Dwelling locations that need GFCI protection
sections.plain_explanation:
In a dwelling, every 125-volt through 250-volt receptacle supplied by a single-phase branch circuit of 150 volts or less to ground needs GFCI protection when it sits in a listed location. Because the rule runs up to 250 V, a 240 V dryer or garage receptacle is covered, not just the 120 V outlets. The NEC 2020 list:
• (1) Bathrooms
• (2) Garages, and accessory buildings with a floor at or below grade not intended as habitable rooms
• (3) Outdoors
• (4) Crawl spaces at or below grade
• (5) Basements
• (6) Kitchens, where receptacles serve countertop surfaces
• (7) Within 6 ft of the top inside edge of a sink bowl
• (8) Boathouses
• (9) Within 6 ft of the outside edge of a bathtub or shower stall
• (10) Laundry areas
• (11) Indoor damp or wet locations
Distances follow the shortest path a cord would take, without piercing a floor, wall, ceiling or fixed barrier and without passing through a door, doorway or window. The GFCI device itself must be readily accessible.
sections.on_the_job: Walk a three-bedroom slab home in Marion Oaks with the plan and number every receptacle, as in the drawing. Under NEC 2020 (permits through Dec 30, 2026): countertop receptacles, the dishwasher outlet (210.8(D)), bath, washer and the 240 V dryer, garage and every outdoor receptacle get GFCI. The refrigerator receptacle 9 ft from the sink and the 240 V range receptacle do not: they serve no countertop and sit outside the 6 ft sink zone. The bedroom receptacle 4 ft from the tub through the wall does not either, because a cord cannot go through a wall. For NEC 2023 permits, the fridge and range outlets join the list.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: protection is at the DFN breaker, so a standard TR receptacle in one of these locations is protected even though the device itself has no test buttons. Do not swap in a GFCI receptacle. Scope note: S-07 covers the 120-volt points on this list. A 240/250-volt point on the list (other than the dryer, which is S-08) takes a 2-pole GFCI breaker — a single-pole DFN cannot protect it.
sections.figure_idea: A bathroom and kitchen plan with 6 ft arcs drawn from a sink edge and from a tub edge, shading every receptacle inside the arcs.

sections.why_it_exists: A fault through a person standing on a wet slab or touching a grounded sink can stop a heart at a current far too small to trip a breaker. A GFCI compares the current leaving on the hot with the current returning on the neutral and opens the circuit when they differ by a few milliamperes (Class A: trips at 6 mA or more, per the informational note to the Article 100 definition).
inspection_fails: 240 V dryer receptacle on a standard 2-pole breaker. The 2020 rule covers 125–250 V receptacles in laundry areas.
Garage receptacle 'just for the freezer' left unprotected. The garage item has no single-appliance exception.
Receptacle within 6 ft of a wet-bar or laundry sink missed because the room is not a kitchen or a bathroom.
Outdoor receptacle on the lanai or under the soffit missed.
GFCI receptacle hidden behind the refrigerator or dishwasher where it is not readily accessible.
sections.exam_trap: A bedroom receptacle is 4 ft from the tub in a straight line, on the other side of the wall. GFCI required? No: the distance is the cord path, and it cannot go through a wall or a doorway. Second trap: in 2020 the sink distance is measured from the top inside edge of the bowl, not from the edge of the counter.

sections.title: Laundry areas — including the dryer receptacle
sections.plain_explanation:
Item (10) on the dwelling list is laundry areas. Read together with the 2020 voltage range in 210.8(A) — 125 volts through 250 volts, single-phase, 150 volts or less to ground — it covers both receptacles in the laundry:
• The 120V washer receptacle
• The 250V dryer receptacle
That is the code reason a modern Sharma dryer circuit needs ground-fault protection even though older Florida houses were built without it. 'Laundry area' means the room or closet where the washer and dryer sit: a laundry room, a laundry closet in a hallway, or the laundry corner of a garage. If the receptacle is in that area, it is on the list, whatever the appliance voltage.
sections.on_the_job: Do not treat the dryer as exempt because it is 240V, and do not protect only the washer outlet. Check the whole laundry area, including a laundry closet in a hallway or garage layout. On a Sharma job the dryer circuit is the Siemens Q230GF, 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker (S-08), so the protection sits in the panel and the dryer receptacle itself is a standard 4-wire device. The washer receptacle gets its GFCI protection at its breaker the same way. Test both at the breaker before the trim-out is signed off.
sections.sharma_note: S-08: dryer circuit is a Siemens Q230GF, 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker. That is the locked Sharma catalog number — do not substitute an older dryer breaker note.
sections.figure_idea: A laundry closet showing a washer receptacle and a 4-wire dryer receptacle, both with a line back to the panel and the 2-pole GFCI breaker highlighted.
sections.why_it_exists: A laundry pairs water, grounded metal appliances and a concrete slab floor — the exact setup that makes a ground fault dangerous. A washer or dryer with an internal fault can put voltage on its metal case while a person touches it with wet hands. GFCI protection watches for current leaking outside the circuit and opens it in a fraction of a second, at 120V or at 250V.
inspection_fails: 250V dryer receptacle on a standard 2-pole breaker with no GFCI protection.
Washer receptacle protected, dryer receptacle in the same laundry closet missed.
Laundry closet in the garage treated as 'not a laundry area' and left unprotected.
GFCI receptacle installed behind the dryer where it is not readily accessible, instead of protection at the breaker.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'the dryer is 240V, so GFCI does not apply — only 120V outlets are on the list.' Wrong for 2020 permits: 210.8(A) runs from 125V through 250V, and laundry areas are item (10). The 240V dryer receptacle needs GFCI protection exactly like the washer.

choices: No — a dedicated appliance is exempt
page_quiz.explain_plain: 210.8(A) covers 125V through 250V receptacles, and laundry areas are item (10).

page_quiz.question: Per Sharma S-08, the dryer circuit is protected by:
choices: A GFCI receptacle behind the dryer
page_quiz.explain_plain: S-08 locks the dryer circuit to the 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker in the panel.

choices: It is not in a laundry area
It needs GFCI protection as a laundry area receptacle

It is exempt as a single appliance outlet
page_quiz.explain_plain: A laundry closet is a laundry area wherever it sits in the dwelling, garage layouts included.

sections.title: GFCI locations outside dwellings
sections.plain_explanation:
Other than dwelling units, GFCI protection is required for receptacles in the locations on the 210.8(B) list. The rule covers 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles on single-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground and 50 amperes or less, and receptacles on three-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground and 100 amperes or less. Those size limits are not the dwelling limits, so a commercial job cannot be roughed in from house habits alone. The NEC 2020 list:
• (1) Bathrooms
• (2) Kitchens, or areas with a sink and permanent provisions for food preparation or cooking
• (3) Rooftops
• (4) Outdoors
• (5) Sinks — receptacles within 6 ft of the top inside edge of the bowl
• (6) Indoor damp or wet locations
• (7) Locker rooms with associated showering facilities
• (8) Garages, accessory buildings, service bays and similar areas, other than vehicle exhibition halls and showrooms
• (9) Crawl spaces at or below grade level
• (10) Unfinished areas of basements
• (11) Laundry areas
• (12) Bathtubs and shower stalls — receptacles within 6 ft of the outside edge of the tub or stall
A commercial kitchen is judged by that sink-and-provisions wording and the equipment in it, not by whether food is sold there.
sections.on_the_job: On a commercial walk, list the wet and outdoor locations from the plans and the equipment schedule, then match each one to this subsection. Flag rooftop and service-bay receptacles early — they are the ones most often added late. On a small Orlando restaurant rough-in, the walk found GFCI needed at the kitchen line, the mop sink, both restrooms, the service bay, and the rooftop unit receptacle — all on 20 A circuits under S-01. The dining room receptacles stayed standard: no sink, no food prep, no place on this list.
sections.sharma_note: S-01 applies on commercial work: 20A minimum branch circuits.

sections.why_it_exists: Commercial spaces put receptacles in the hands of employees and the public, often on wet concrete, at sinks, and outdoors where nobody maintains them. A ground fault through a person standing on a wet service-bay floor can be fatal at a current no breaker will notice. GFCI protection watches for that lost current and opens the circuit in a fraction of a cycle.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is roughing a shop from the dwelling list. A receptacle on a rooftop, in a service bay, or in a locker room with showers needs GFCI here even though none of those rooms is on the house list — and a break room with a sink and a microwave counts as a kitchen area under (B)(2) even though no food is sold.
inspection_fails: Rooftop receptacle serving the HVAC unit on a standard breaker. Rooftops are (B)(3).
Service-bay receptacles left unprotected because 'it is not a dwelling garage.' (B)(8) covers service bays.
Receptacle 4 ft from the mop sink on a standard breaker. Within 6 ft of a sink is (B)(5).
Break-room receptacles missed because no food is sold there. A sink plus permanent food-prep provisions makes it a (B)(2) kitchen area.
Locker-room receptacles by the showers unprotected. Locker rooms with showering facilities are (B)(7).

sections.title: Specific appliances that need GFCI protection
sections.plain_explanation:
Beyond the location lists, this subsection points to 422.5(A): specific appliances need ground-fault protection wherever they are installed, in any occupancy, when rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amps or less. The 2020 list:
• Automotive vacuum machines
• Drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations
• Cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washers
• Tire inflation machines
• Vending machines
• Sump pumps
• Dishwashers
The test is the appliance and its rating, not the room. When an appliance is on the list, moving it to a room that is not on the 210.8(A) list does not remove the requirement. The dishwasher is the one a house crew meets every week: it needs this protection in a dwelling, a restaurant or an office kitchen, whether it plugs in or is hardwired.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma spec home in Marion Oaks, the dishwasher is the standing case: it lands on a 20 A kitchen circuit, and the S-07 dual-function breaker in the Siemens panel supplies the GFCI protection, with a standard TR receptacle under the sink where the dishwasher plugs in. The site trap is the appliance swap: the builder changes the dishwasher model after trim and nobody rechecks. Because the protection lives at the breaker, the new unit is covered the moment it is plugged in. On a small commercial job, check the vending machine and the bottle fill station the same way: both are on the 422.5(A) list even though the break room is not a 210.8(A) location.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: a DFN breaker supplies this protection on 120V circuits, with a standard TR receptacle at the appliance where there is a receptacle.

nec2023_change.change: 210.8(D) now names the appliances: electric ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers and microwave ovens were added, correlated with 422.5(A).
nec2023_change.source: Georgia DCA 2023 NEC changes presentation (slide 'Specific Appliances'); Electrical Exam Coach 210.8

sections.why_it_exists: Every appliance on this list mixes electricity with water, wet hands or a wet floor. A sump pump sits in a pit of water, a spray washer soaks its operator, and a dishwasher can leak across a kitchen floor. A fault inside the appliance can put full line voltage on its metal case, and the person who touches it becomes the path to ground. GFCI protection watches for current leaking where it should not go and opens the circuit in a fraction of a second, before that case can deliver a dangerous shock.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "The break room is not on the 210.8(A) list, so the vending machine needs no GFCI." Wrong — 210.8(D) follows the appliance, not the room, in any occupancy. Second trap: picking an electric range or a clothes dryer as a 2020 requirement. Those appliances were added in 2023; under the 2020 rule above they are not on the (D) list.
inspection_fails: Dishwasher on a standard breaker with no GFCI protection — the most common 210.8(D) write-up there is.
Sump pump on an unprotected receptacle because the pit closet "is not a listed location."
Vending machine or bottle fill station on an unprotected circuit in a commercial break room.
GFCI protection taken out after nuisance trips instead of finding the faulting appliance.

sections.title: Outdoor outlets other than receptacles
sections.plain_explanation: This subsection reaches outdoor outlets that are not receptacles — a point where current is taken for equipment, such as the disconnect feeding a hardwired condenser. For dwellings, all outdoor outlets other than those already covered as outdoor receptacles need GFCI protection for personnel when supplied by a single-phase branch circuit rated 150 volts or less to ground and 50 amperes or less. The NEC's own exception covers lighting outlets other than those in 210.8(C). For a one- or two-family dwelling, Florida resolves the condenser question directly: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment.
sections.on_the_job: Check the circuit rating first: on a dwelling, a single-phase circuit at 150 volts or less to ground and 50 amperes or less puts a hardwired outdoor outlet in this rule. Listed HVAC on a house falls under the Florida exception; plan on GFCI protection for other outdoor equipment. A 3-ton condenser on a 35 A breaker sits inside those rating limits, so the Florida exception is the only reason it rides on a standard 2-pole breaker — Sharma practice, confirmed with the AHJ, not a blanket NEC exemption.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice (tip, not an S-rule): condensers are normally on a standard 2-pole breaker sized to the nameplate maximum overcurrent protection. Confirm the AHJ — do not present that practice as a code exemption.

sections.title: Branch circuits a dwelling must have
sections.plain_explanation:
210.11 is the circuit-count backbone of a dwelling, and it works in layers:
• Enough circuits for the load. The number of branch circuits is set by the total calculated load and the size of the circuits used, and the load must be spread evenly among them — not stacked on the first few breakers in the panel (210.11(A) and (B)).
• The named dwelling circuits of 210.11(C). At least two 20 A small-appliance circuits serve kitchen, pantry, breakfast and dining receptacles. At least one 20 A circuit serves the laundry area. At least one 20 A circuit serves bathroom receptacles. And 2020 adds a dedicated 20 A garage circuit for the required garage receptacles. Each named circuit carries tight limits on what else it may feed; the next page works through them.
• Everything else: general lighting and receptacle circuits, plus the individual circuits other articles require for specific equipment.
A panel schedule that only counts spare spaces has not answered this section — the named circuits have to exist, be the right size, and serve the right outlets.
sections.on_the_job: Build the panel schedule for a Marion Oaks spec house from this section outward. The first lines are the named circuits: two 20 A small-appliance circuits to the kitchen and dining receptacles, one 20 A laundry circuit, one 20 A bathroom circuit and one 20 A garage circuit — five circuits before a single general circuit is counted. Then come the general lighting and receptacle circuits with the load spread evenly, then the individual appliance circuits, then spares. Sharma practice on houses is modest 15 A area circuits for lights, fans and general receptacles, reserving 20 A circuits for the required dedicated loads; on commercial work S-01 reverses that, making 20 A the minimum. If a named circuit is feeding lights or another room, that is a rough-in error, not a labeling fix.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma often uses modest 15A area circuits for lights, fans, and general receptacles and reserves 20A circuits for the required dedicated loads. That is company practice, not a code minimum — and S-01 reverses it on commercial work.
sections.figure_idea: A draft panel schedule with the four named dwelling circuits highlighted at the top and general circuits below.

nec2023_change.change: The required 20-amp garage receptacle circuit is no longer limited to the required receptacles, added receptacles can use their own 15-amp-or-larger circuits, and one-bay garages can share it with equipment. The required 20-amp circuit can now serve every garage receptacle, not just the required ones, but still no other kinds of outlets.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.11 Garage receptacle circuit

sections.why_it_exists: Houses fail here in a familiar way: one circuit ends up carrying the microwave, the toaster oven and the hair dryer because nobody planned the count. Overloaded circuits run hot inside walls and trip in daily use, and occupants answer with extension cords and space heaters plugged in wherever they fit. Naming the circuits up front — 20 A, and fenced off from other outlets — puts the hardest-used receptacles in the house on circuits built for them.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is stretching the single-bathroom allowance: one 20 A circuit may carry one bathroom's receptacles and that same bathroom's other outlets — it may not carry two bathrooms. Second trap: counting spaces. A panel with spare spaces available does not satisfy 210.11 when the laundry receptacle is riding a general circuit; the named circuit has to exist.
inspection_fails: Laundry receptacle on a general lighting circuit — no 20 A laundry branch circuit exists.
One 20 A circuit serving receptacle outlets in two bathrooms.
Small-appliance circuit feeding a bedroom or living-room receptacle.
Garage receptacles tapped off a general circuit; no dedicated 20 A garage circuit (2020).
Load stacked on a few circuits at the top of the panel with the rest empty — not spread evenly among the branch circuits.

sections.title: The named dwelling circuits: kitchen, laundry, bathroom, garage
sections.plain_explanation: This subsection names four things. At least two 20A small-appliance circuits serve kitchen, pantry, breakfast, and dining receptacles, with tight limits on other outlets. At least one 20A laundry circuit serves the laundry receptacle and nothing else outside that area. At least one 20A bathroom circuit serves bathroom receptacles, or — for a single bathroom only — may carry that bathroom's other outlets. And the 2020 edition adds a dedicated 20A garage circuit for the required garage receptacles, with a limited allowance for readily accessible outdoor receptacles.
sections.on_the_job: Panel schedule for a three-bed, two-bath Florida spec house, labeled by code job: spaces 1 and 3 'SABC KITCHEN 1 / 2', space 5 'LAUNDRY — NO OTHER OUTLETS', space 7 'BATH RECEP', space 9 'GARAGE RECEP', and S-06 puts the microwave on its own 20A circuit at space 11. Before trim-out, walk the 'no other outlets' limits: the laundry circuit stops at the laundry room wall, and the bath circuit serves one bathroom's receptacles — the single-bathroom exception does not let it carry the second bathroom's receptacles plus lights.
sections.sharma_note: S-06 sits on top of this list: the microwave gets its own 20A circuit, separate from the small-appliance circuits. The wire size is PENDING (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA).

The 'no other outlets' limits are what make the protection predictable.

sections.title: Arc-fault protection
sections.plain_explanation:
Arc-fault protection guards against damaged, pinched or deteriorating wiring and loose connections that can arc — sparking across a gap or through damaged insulation — long before a breaker sees an overload. For dwelling units, 210.12(A) applies to 120 V, single-phase, 15 A and 20 A branch circuits that supply outlets or devices in the listed rooms:
• Kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms, parlors, libraries, dens and bedrooms
• Sunrooms, recreation rooms, closets, hallways, laundry areas, and similar rooms or areas
Bathrooms, garages and unfinished basements are not on the list, and a 240 V appliance circuit is outside the subsection's stated range. The protection may be provided by a listed combination-type AFCI breaker, or by one of the other arrangements the section permits — what matters is that the outlets in the listed rooms end up protected. Arc-fault and ground-fault protection do different jobs; one does not replace the other.
sections.on_the_job: Think of this as a room list applied at the panel. On a Sharma house the question is answered before it is asked: S-07 puts a dual-function breaker on every 120 V circuit, so the kitchen, bedroom, hallway, closet and laundry circuits in a Marion Oaks spec house are AFCI protected without sorting rooms at trim. Where that standard is not in play — a panel change on an older home that keeps the existing panel, for example — mark every 15 A and 20 A 120 V circuit on the schedule with the rooms it serves and test the list against 210.12(A). When a plan adds a room or changes a room's use, re-check the list instead of copying the last house's schedule.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: Sharma's dual-function breaker provides both arc-fault and ground-fault protection on every 120V circuit, so the room-by-room question is answered at the breaker for standard house work.
sections.figure_idea: A cutaway wall showing a nail through a cable with a small arc, and the breaker in the panel sensing the arcing signature.
sections.why_it_exists: An arc at a loose terminal, or where a nail has nicked a cable, can glow hot enough to ignite wood, bedding or insulation while drawing less current than the load itself — far below the level that trips a standard breaker. The AFCI watches for the electrical signature of arcing and opens the circuit before the arc becomes a fire. That is why the room list covers the rooms where people sleep, sit and store things.
inspection_fails: Kitchen small-appliance circuit on a standard breaker. Kitchens are on the 210.12(A) list.
Hallway or closet circuit missed because the plan called the space 'storage.' Closets and similar areas are listed.
AFCI breaker swapped for a standard breaker after nuisance-trip complaints, with no correction of the arcing fault it was reporting.
GFCI-only breaker installed where AFCI was required, 'because it also protects.' Ground-fault protection is not arc-fault protection.
Bedroom circuit protected only at a receptacle device that is not part of an arrangement 210.12 permits for the wiring method used.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the bathroom: it is on the GFCI list, so it feels like it belongs on every protection list — but 210.12(A) does not list bathrooms, garages or unfinished basements. The reverse trap fails answers too: a GFCI breaker by itself does not satisfy an AFCI requirement. The two protections watch for different failures.

sections.title: Rooms where dwelling circuits need AFCI protection
sections.plain_explanation:
For dwellings, this subsection applies to 120V, single-phase, 15A and 20A branch circuits supplying outlets or devices in the listed rooms and areas:
• Kitchens
• Family rooms
• Dining rooms
• Living rooms
• Parlors
• Libraries
• Dens
• Bedrooms
• Sunrooms
• Recreation rooms
• Closets
• Hallways
• Laundry areas
• Similar rooms or areas
Read the list by what is missing: a bathroom, a garage, and an unfinished basement are not on it, so a circuit that serves only those areas is outside this subsection. The rating limits matter too: a 240V appliance circuit is outside this subsection's stated range. The protection may be a listed combination-type AFCI breaker or one of the other arrangements 210.12 permits, but every outlet and device a covered circuit supplies in a listed room must end up protected.
sections.on_the_job: On the panel schedule, mark every 15A and 20A 120V circuit with the rooms it serves, then test that list against this subsection. Mixed circuits that touch a listed room need the protection for the whole circuit. On a Marion Oaks rough-in that means the bedroom, living and family room circuits, the hall and closet lighting, and the laundry circuit all land on AFCI protection — while the bathroom circuit, the garage circuit, and the 240V range and dryer circuits are not covered by this subsection. Sharma's S-07 dual-function breakers cover the 120V list by default, so the schedule check is a confirmation, not a redesign.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 already puts a dual-function breaker on every 120V circuit, which is stricter and simpler than sorting rooms at trim. Keep it that way unless Sanjay directs otherwise on a specific job.
sections.why_it_exists: Most house fires of electrical origin start with arcing: a cord pinched behind furniture, a staple driven too tight, a loose connection heating and spitting sparks into dust and framing. A standard breaker sees none of it, because a series arc can draw less current than the circuit rating. AFCI protection watches the waveform for the signature of arcing and opens the circuit before the arc becomes a fire.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer adds the bathroom and the garage to the AFCI list by mixing it up with the GFCI list in 210.8. The two lists are different: bathrooms and garages need GFCI protection, but they are not on the 210.12(A) AFCI list. Second trap: protecting only the bedroom receptacles on a circuit that also feeds the hall light. If any part of the circuit serves a listed room, the circuit needs the protection.
inspection_fails: Bedroom circuit landed on a standard breaker — no AFCI protection at final.
Laundry-area circuit missed because the room was treated as a utility space, not a listed area.
Remodel circuit extended well past 6 ft with no AFCI protection added (210.12(D)).
AFCI breaker protecting only part of a circuit that also serves a listed room from an unprotected tap.

sections.title: Extending or modifying an existing circuit
sections.plain_explanation: Where branch-circuit wiring in any area covered by 210.12(A), (B), or (C) — dwelling units, dormitory units, and guest rooms and guest suites — is modified, replaced, or extended, the circuit must gain AFCI protection. It may be protected by any of the methods in 210.12(A)(1) through (6), or by a listed outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle outlet of the existing circuit. One narrow exception: no AFCI is required where the extension of the existing conductors is not more than 6 ft and adds no outlets or devices other than splicing devices; conductor length inside an enclosure, cabinet, or junction box does not count toward the 6 ft.
sections.on_the_job: On service work, measure the extension before assuming the exception saves you: 6 ft or less, splices only, and no new outlet or device. Anything longer, or anything added, means AFCI — one of the 210.12(A) methods, or an outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle.

nec2023_change.change: AFCI now reaches sleeping quarters at stations for fire, police, ambulance, rescue and ranger crews, and 10-amp circuits join the 15-amp and 20-amp circuits that need it. Rooms used only for sleeping at stations for fire, police, ambulance, rescue or ranger crews, and similar places, now need AFCI (210.12(D)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.12 AFCI protection

sections.why_it_exists: An old circuit does not get safer because the job was small. Moving a receptacle, adding a light, or extending a run disturbs exactly the connections and insulation that arc faults start from — and the rest of the circuit is still older wiring with no protection. The rule closes the door on 'we only touched a little of it' by making the protection follow the modification, not the size of the job.
inspection_fails: Receptacle relocated 10 ft on an existing bedroom circuit with no AFCI protection added.
New recessed lights tapped off an existing living-room circuit; the circuit left on a standard breaker.
A 5 ft extension with a new receptacle added, claimed under the 6 ft exception — the added outlet kills the exception.
Outlet branch-circuit AFCI installed at the second receptacle instead of the first receptacle outlet of the circuit.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reading the 6 ft exception too loosely. It saves you only when the extension is 6 ft or less AND nothing but splicing devices is added. Add one receptacle at the end of a 5 ft extension and the exception is gone — the circuit needs AFCI protection. The other wrong answer is protecting only the new piece: the protection covers the modified circuit, by a 210.12(A) method or an outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle outlet.

sections.title: Sizing branch-circuit conductors
sections.plain_explanation: Conductors and breakers for a branch circuit are sized for the load the circuit will actually carry, and a continuous load — one that runs at its maximum for three hours or more — is counted at 125 percent for that sizing unless the assembly is listed for continuous operation at its rating. That is why a load that looks like it 'fits' a breaker on nameplate amps alone can still need the next size up. Multi-outlet circuits supplying receptacles for cord-and-plug loads are also sized by the rating rules in this section and in 210.23.
sections.on_the_job:
Find the continuous loads first: EV charging, fixed heating, some lighting and equipment. Do the 125 percent math on paper in the job file, not in your head at the supply counter.

Worked example: a 16A continuous load counts 16 × 1.25 = 20A, so both the conductor ampacity and the breaker land at 20A minimum. A 24A continuous load counts 30A the same way — which is why an EV charger nameplate that 'fits' a smaller breaker on its face still sizes the circuit up.
sections.sharma_note: S-01: commercial branch circuits are 20A minimum with 12 AWG copper minimum at Sharma, whatever the general sizing math would allow at 15A.
sections.figure_idea: A worked example strip: 16A continuous load, times 1.25, equals a 20A circuit — with the breaker and the conductor both stepped up.

nec2023_change.change: Clarified that the voltage limitation should apply to the circuit, not the conductor insulation rating, and specified that Section 210.19 applies to branch circuits not exceeding 1000 volts ac or 1500 volts dc.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 210.19 Conductors - Minimum Ampacity and Size

sections.why_it_exists: Heat is the slow enemy of a branch circuit. A continuous load holds conductors and breaker terminals at full temperature for hours, and insulation ages and connections loosen with every hot cycle. Counting the load at 125 percent builds in headroom: the circuit runs at 80 percent of its rating, so a load that never shuts off does not cook the wire or nuisance-trip the breaker.
inspection_fails: EV charger delivering 48 A on a 50 A breaker — a continuous load that counts 60 A.
Fixed electric heat wired at nameplate amps with no 125 percent factor on the conductor.
Breaker stepped up for a continuous load but the conductor left at the old size.
Commercial lighting loaded to a full 20 A continuous on a 20 A breaker and conductor.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the breaker to the nameplate: a 24 A continuous load on a 25 A breaker 'because it fits.' It does not fit — the load counts 30 A, so the conductor ampacity and the breaker both land at 30 A minimum. Nameplate amps are the starting number, never the answer, for a continuous load.

sections.title: Outlet devices and receptacle ratings on a circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
This section matches the device to the circuit: lampholders, receptacles, and cord-and-plug equipment may not be loaded beyond their own ratings, and a receptacle's rating must fit the circuit it sits on. On a 20A multi-outlet circuit, 15A duplex receptacles are permitted because the load is spread across outlets; a single receptacle on an individual 20A circuit is a different case and must match the circuit. The existing lookup item carries the rating table in plain form.

The rating match, from Table 210.21(B)(3) — where a circuit feeds two or more receptacles, the receptacle rating may be:
• 15A circuit — receptacles not over 15A
• 20A circuit — 15A or 20A receptacles
• 30A circuit — 30A receptacles
• 40A circuit — 40A or 50A receptacles
• 50A circuit — 50A receptacles
A single receptacle on an individual branch circuit must be rated not less than the circuit. And the most one cord-and-plug load may draw on a multi-outlet circuit (Table 210.21(B)(2)):
• 15A circuit — 12A
• 20A circuit — 16A
• 30A circuit — 24A
sections.on_the_job: When a plan calls for a single dedicated receptacle — a fridge, a microwave, a shop tool — check the device rating against the circuit rating before trim. Do not let a trim bin of 15A devices decide the question. On trim in a Lake County kitchen, the microwave's individual 20A circuit gets a single 20A receptacle — a 15A duplex out of the trim bin fails the match, even though the same device is fine on the shared countertop circuits (S-06).
sections.sharma_note: S-06: the microwave's individual 20A circuit pairs with that sizing check.
sections.edition_note:

sections.why_it_exists: A receptacle is the weakest link a load plugs into. If a device is rated below what the circuit can deliver, the device — not the breaker — becomes the fuse: contacts overheat inside the box where nobody sees it. Matching the receptacle rating to the circuit, and capping what one cord-and-plug load may draw, keeps the breaker as the device that opens first.

20A receptacle installed on a 15A circuit.

Lampholder or outlet device loaded beyond its own rating.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: '15A receptacles are never allowed on a 20A circuit.' They are — where the circuit feeds two or more receptacles, Table 210.21(B)(3) allows 15A or 20A devices. The trap's other side is that same 15A duplex used as the single receptacle on an individual 20A circuit. There it must be rated not less than the circuit: 20A.

sections.title: How much load a branch circuit may carry
sections.plain_explanation:
This section caps what may be put on a circuit by its rating. Any one cord-and-plug-connected utilization equipment not fastened in place may not take more than 80 percent of the branch-circuit rating (12A on 15A, 16A on 20A) on any 15A or 20A branch circuit, and fastened-in-place equipment has its own limit when it shares a circuit with lighting or portable loads. Motor and specific-appliance loads are sent to their own articles instead of being judged by a general percentage.

The percentages in amperes:
• A cord-and-plug appliance that is not fastened in place, on a circuit that also serves other outlets — not over 80 percent of the circuit rating: 12A on a 15A circuit, 16A on a 20A circuit
• Fastened-in-place equipment sharing a circuit with lighting outlets or portable cord-and-plug loads — not over 50 percent of the circuit rating: 7.5A on a 15A circuit, 10A on a 20A circuit
A circuit that serves only its own fastened equipment is judged by the equipment's own article and nameplate, not by these shared-circuit caps.
sections.on_the_job: Do the percentage math for the big plug-in loads: space heaters, window units, and shop equipment are where a shared 20A circuit quietly goes over. If a load is fastened in place and shares the circuit, check the second limit too. Run the numbers on the heater: a 1,500W space heater pulls 12.5A at 120V. Alone on a 20A circuit it fits the 16A cap; on a 15A circuit it is already over the 12A cap before anything else is plugged in.

nec2023_change.change: Only three things fit a 10-amp circuit: lighting, a dwelling bath or laundry fan on that room's lights, and a lone gas fireplace. Receptacles, laundry equipment, garage door openers and other fixed appliances stay off. Lighting outlets are the main job for a 10-amp branch circuit.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.23 What a 10-amp circuit can feed

sections.why_it_exists: Plug-in loads are the ones nobody calculates. A space heater or window unit can sit at full draw for hours, and on a shared circuit it stacks on top of everything else plugged in that day. The 80 percent cap leaves headroom so one portable load cannot cook the circuit by itself; the 50 percent cap on fastened equipment protects the lighting and portable loads that share its circuit from being crowded out.

sections.exam_trap: The trap: using the 80 percent number for everything. Fastened-in-place equipment that shares a circuit with lighting or portable loads is capped at 50 percent, not 80 — 10A on a 20A circuit, 7.5A on a 15A circuit. Eighty percent is only for the one cord-and-plug load that is not fastened in place.

sections.title: Where dwelling receptacles must go
sections.plain_explanation:
210.52 decides where a dwelling must have receptacle outlets, so every lamp and appliance reaches one without an extension cord. Two rules drive most rough-ins:
• Wall spaces, 210.52(A): in kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms, dens, sunrooms, bedrooms, recreation rooms and similar rooms, no point along the floor line of any wall space may be more than 6 ft from a receptacle. That works out to 12 ft maximum between receptacles. Measure along the floor line; corners do not break the wall, but doorways, fireplaces and fixed cabinets without countertops do. Any wall space 2 ft or wider counts, including fixed glass panels and fixed room dividers; sliding panels do not.
• Countertops, 210.52(C): each wall counter space 12 in or wider gets a receptacle, and no point along the wall line may be more than 24 in from one, so 48 in maximum between them. Ranges, cooktops, sinks and refrigerators split a counter into separate spaces. Countertop receptacles sit no more than 20 in above the counter.
Receptacles more than 5½ ft above the floor, inside cabinets, or built into a luminaire or appliance do not count toward the required outlets.
sections.on_the_job: Living room in a Marion Oaks spec house, 14 ft × 16 ft with one entry door. Start at the door jamb, measure 6 ft along the floor line, set the first box, then one every 12 ft or less around the room, around the corners, until you come back to the other jamb. That is five boxes, as drawn. In the kitchen, rough each counter piece on its own: the 3 ft piece between the sink and the range needs a receptacle, and so does the 15 in piece on the far side of the range. On an island, count the square footage from the countertop drawing before the cabinets arrive.
sections.sharma_note: S-04: where the plan is silent, receptacles are set 18 in to the bottom of the box. That is a Sharma standard, not a number from this section — countertop limits in 210.52(C) are code and are different.
sections.figure_idea: A floor plan with a receptacle symbol being placed along every wall, counter, and hallway in sequence.

nec2023_change.change: Dwelling kitchen islands and peninsulas don't need a receptacle anymore, and no countertop receptacle can sit below the top. Skip the island receptacle and you still leave provisions for one later. A receptacle at a kitchen island or peninsula is now optional.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 210.52 Island receptacles now optional

sections.title: Wall spacing in habitable rooms
sections.plain_explanation: In kitchens, family rooms, bedrooms, and the other rooms this subsection lists, receptacles are placed so that no point along the floor line of a wall is more than 6 ft from a receptacle — which works out to 12 ft maximum between receptacles on a run (210.52(A)(1)). Measure along the floor line and around corners: corners do not break a wall run, but doorways, fireplaces, and fixed cabinets without countertops do. Wall space is counted from 2 ft wide upward, and fixed panels and fixed room dividers count as wall space while sliding panels do not (210.52(A)(2)). A floor receptacle counts only when it sits within 18 in of the wall (210.52(A)(3)), and a receptacle more than 5½ ft above the floor, inside a cabinet, or behind a fixed appliance does not do the job this spacing is meant to do.
sections.on_the_job: Bedroom wall in a Marion Oaks spec house, 26 ft long with a 3 ft door opening: measure along the floor line from the first jamb. First run, 10 ft: one receptacle near the middle puts every point within 6 ft. Second run, 13 ft: two receptacles, at about 6 ft and 12 ft from the jamb, cover the end of the wall. Then mark the pieces crews skip — the 2 ft stub between the closet door and the corner is wall space and needs coverage. Set the boxes at S-04 height, 18 in to the bottom of the box, and walk the wall with a tape before you drill a single hole.
sections.sharma_note: S-04 sets the box height when the plan is silent: 18 in to the bottom of the box. S-05 sets switch boxes at 48 in to center under the same condition.

sections.why_it_exists: The rule is written around the length of a lamp or appliance cord. If every point on the wall is within 6 ft of a receptacle, cords reach without extension cords — and extension cords run under rugs and through doorways are a standing fire and trip hazard. The 2 ft rule exists because the short wall piece beside a door is exactly where a lamp or a vacuum wants to plug in.

Corners do not break wall space — the measurement follows the floor line around the corner, so a receptacle just past the corner can cover the end of the wall before it. Doorways are the opposite: they break the run and the 6 ft count starts over at the jamb.

sections.title: Small-appliance circuits — what they may feed
sections.plain_explanation: The two (or more) 20A small-appliance branch circuits serve the receptacle outlets in the kitchen, pantry, breakfast room and dining room — and only those. A receptacle for refrigeration equipment in those rooms may ride on one of them. The only other outlets allowed are a clock receptacle and receptacles used for supplemental equipment on a gas-fired range, oven or cooktop. A receptacle in the living room, a bathroom receptacle, or the kitchen lighting may not be added to these circuits, and these circuits may not wander off to feed outlets in other rooms. Refrigeration equipment may instead be fed from an individual branch circuit rated 15A or more (210.52(B)(1) Exception No. 2).
sections.on_the_job: Lay out the two circuits before rough-in so the countertop receptacles alternate between them (that layout rule is on the 210.52(C) page). Sharma rule S-06 puts the microwave on its own 20A circuit. Code-wise, a countertop microwave may plug into a small-appliance circuit; a fastened-in-place over-the-range microwave may not be fed from one (210.52(B)(2)).
sections.figure_idea: Kitchen plan with receptacles colored by circuit: countertop outlets split between SA-1 and SA-2, the fridge on SA-1, the microwave on its own circuit.

sections.why_it_exists: Countertop appliances are the heaviest portable loads in the house — kettles, toasters, air fryers, coffee makers — and two of them on one circuit is a normal breakfast. Keeping the small-appliance circuits exclusive to the food-prep rooms means those loads never share a circuit with lighting or with receptacles across the house, and the two circuits can be balanced along the counter. Let one of these circuits wander, and both the protection and the load spreading the rule was built on are gone.

Only one 20A small-appliance circuit provided for the kitchen receptacles.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the refrigerator: many pick 'the fridge can never be on a small-appliance circuit.' It may — or it can have its own individual branch circuit rated 15A or more. The real bars are the kitchen lighting and a fastened-in-place microwave: neither may ride on these circuits.
