sections.title: Outside branch circuits and feeders
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 225 covers wiring that runs outside — between buildings, across a yard, or overhead or underground to a detached structure. Sharma meets it on detached garages, barns, pool houses and site lighting fed from a house or a main building. Its recurring themes:
• One supply: a building or structure gets a single feeder or branch circuit, or a single set of feeders, subject to the exceptions the section lists — and where an exception adds a supply, the building carries a permanent plaque or directory showing where the other disconnects are (225.30).
• A disconnect at the building being supplied, in a readily accessible location outside the building or inside nearest the point where the conductors enter (225.31, 225.32). The supply may be disconnected by up to six grouped, marked switches or breakers (225.33, 225.34), and a feeder disconnect serving a one-family dwelling is rated at least 100 A (225.39(C)).
• Clearances: overhead conductors keep the clearances of 225.18 — 10 ft over areas subject only to pedestrian traffic, 12 ft over residential driveways, 18 ft over roads, streets and areas subject to truck traffic — judged at final sag.
• Sealed entries: raceways entering a building from outside still get sealed (225.27).
sections.on_the_job: Detached two-car garage behind a Belleview house, fed from the house panel. One feeder — not two — crosses the yard underground to the garage, where the building disconnect sits at the wall nearest the point where the feeder enters, rated 100 A as 225.39(C) requires for a one-family dwelling, and the garage gets its own grounding treatment under 250.32. Flown overhead across the driveway instead, the same feeder would need 12 ft of clearance at final sag. When a run leaves a building, switch articles: a feeder inside one building and the same feeder continued to a second building are judged by different pages, and the second building needs its own disconnect and grounding treatment.
sections.figure_idea: A site plan: house panel, a buried feeder crossing a yard, and a detached garage with its own disconnect and ground rods.

nec2023_change.change: New 225.41: an outdoor emergency disconnect is required for one- and two-family dwellings supplied by a feeder (mirrors 230.85). New 225.42: SPD on feeders supplying dwelling-type occupancies. 225.5 (size of conductors) and 225.7 (lighting equipment on poles) were deleted.
nec2023_change.source: Knoxville 'Significant Changes to the 2023 NEC' (Clay Taylor); Carosella 2023 NEC workbook

nec2023_change.change: Raceways coming into a building from outside still get sealed. New in 2023, the rule says how: the seal has to meet both 300.5(G) and 300.7(A). The seal now has to satisfy 300.5(G), the underground raceway seal rule, and 300.7(A), the rule for raceways passing from warm to cold.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 225.27 Raceway seals at building entries

sections.why_it_exists: Outside wiring lives a harder life: sun, storm wind, ladders, vehicles and shovels all find it. The one-supply rule and the disconnect at the far building exist for the emergency case — a person at the detached building must be able to kill its power there, and must be able to trust that the disconnect really kills all of it. A second, forgotten supply leaves a 'dead' building live.
inspection_fails: Two ordinary feeders run to the same detached garage because two panels were convenient — no 225.30 exception, and no plaque.
No disconnect at the detached building; the only way to kill its power is the breaker back at the house.
Building disconnect mounted across the building from where the feeder enters, instead of nearest the point of entrance.
Overhead span sagging below 12 ft over the residential driveway at final sag.
Underground raceway entering the building unsealed (225.27).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the breaker back at the house as the detached building's disconnect. It is not: 225.31 requires a disconnecting means at the building being supplied. The second trap is rating that disconnect 60 A on a one-family dwelling — 60 A is 225.39(D), 'all others'; a one-family dwelling feeder disconnect is 100 A minimum under 225.39(C).

sections.title: Clearances for outside overhead conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors run overhead outside — a feeder across a yard to a detached garage is Sharma's common case — must clear what is under and beside them. The vertical clearances from this section, measured at the conductor's lowest point:
• Over roofs — not a 225.18 item: roof clearance is 225.19(A), 8 ft 6 in., with the reductions listed there
• Over areas subject only to pedestrian traffic, at 150 V or less to ground — 10 ft
• Over residential property and driveways, and commercial areas not subject to truck traffic, at 300 V or less to ground — 12 ft
• Over those same residential and commercial areas where the voltage exceeds 300 V to ground — 15 ft
• Over public streets, alleys, roads, parking areas subject to truck traffic, driveways on other than residential property, and other land traversed by vehicles (cultivated, grazing, forest, orchard) — 18 ft
• Over track rails — 24-1/2 ft
Clearance is judged at final sag, not at the height the conductor left the pole or mast on a cool morning.
sections.on_the_job: Walk the span before you set the attachment heights: the same garage feeder is a 10 ft job over the lawn, a 12 ft job where it crosses the driveway, and an 18 ft job if it crosses the street. The highest number on the route sets the attachment. On a Marion Oaks garage feeder, set the mast and the garage attachment so the lowest point of the span at final sag — a still, hot afternoon, not the cool morning you strung it — clears the street at 18 ft, and the driveway and lawn numbers take care of themselves.
sections.figure_idea: A yard feeder span in profile crossing lawn, driveway, and street edge, with 10 ft, 12 ft, and 18 ft clearance lines drawn under it.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A conductor is not a fixed line in the air. It sags lower on a hot afternoon under load, swings in wind, and gets closer to whatever is under it. The clearances are the air gap that keeps a raised dump bed, an aluminum ladder, a pool pole, or a person standing in a truck bed from touching an energized conductor. Air is the insulation here — the numbers are how much of it the Code demands over each kind of surface.
inspection_fails: Feeder over a residential driveway at 11 ft at final sag — 12 ft minimum.
Clearance checked at the mast on a cool morning; mid-span sag on a hot afternoon put the conductor under the minimum.
Span crossing the street to a detached garage held to the 12 ft driveway number instead of 18 ft over the road.
Conductor over a parking lot used by delivery trucks at 15 ft — truck traffic takes the 18 ft number.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering 12 ft for every residential span. Twelve feet is the driveway number. The same conductor needs 18 ft over the street and only 10 ft over lawn open just to pedestrians — and the highest number on the route is the one that sets the attachment height. And 15 ft is not the vehicle-land number — it is the 12 ft areas when the voltage goes over 300 V to ground.

sections.title: How many supplies may feed one building
sections.plain_explanation:
The general rule is one: a building or other structure gets a single feeder or branch circuit, or a single set of feeders. A multiwire branch circuit counts as a single circuit here. Additional supplies are permitted only through the exceptions:
• (A) Special conditions: fire pumps, emergency systems, legally required standby, optional standby, parallel power production, and systems designed for connection to multiple sources for enhanced reliability
• (B) Special occupancies, by special permission: multiple-occupancy buildings where there is no space for supply equipment accessible to all occupants, or a single building large enough to need two or more supplies
• (C) Capacity requirements: the capacity needed is in excess of 2000 A at a supply voltage of 600 V or less
• (D) Different characteristics: different voltages, frequencies or phases, or different uses
• (E) Documented switching procedures: installations under single management with documented safe switching procedures established and maintained
Two ordinary feeders run to the same detached garage because two panels were convenient is not one of the cases. Where an exception is used, the building must carry a permanent plaque or directory showing where the other disconnects are.
sections.on_the_job: A homeowner in Ocala wants a second 100 A feeder to the workshop for a welder, on top of the 100 A feeder already feeding it. No exception covers that — convenience is not on the list. Before running a second supply to a structure that already has one, name the exception in writing in the job file. If you cannot name one, redesign to a single larger feeder and a subpanel with room to grow. When a standby generator is added later, that supply rides on (A) — with its own disconnect, and the plaque at the building updated to show it.
sections.why_it_exists: Every extra supply is another way for a building to stay live after someone thinks it is dead. A firefighter, or the next electrician, opens the disconnect they can see — and the second feeder, run for convenience and documented nowhere, keeps the building energized. One supply, or a plaque that names the rest, is what makes 'off' mean off.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'Each feeder has its own disconnect, so two feeders to one building are fine.' Wrong — disconnects do not create the permission. Without an exception in (A) through (E), the building gets one supply no matter how neatly the second one is installed. Runner-up trap: counting a multiwire branch circuit as two supplies. It counts as one circuit.
inspection_fails: Second feeder to a detached garage with no 225.30 exception — 'the owner wanted the welder separate' is not an exception.
Standby supply added under an exception, but no plaque or directory at the building showing where the other disconnect is.
Disconnects for two supplies scattered around the building, not grouped or identified.
Two supplies under single management with no documented switching procedure, where (E) was the claimed basis.

sections.title: A disconnect at the building being supplied
sections.plain_explanation:
A feeder or branch circuit supplying another building or structure must have a disconnecting means at that building (225.31). The disconnect opens all ungrounded conductors that supply or pass through the building, so a person at the detached building can kill its power without walking back to the main building.
How many disconnects there may be, how they sit, and how big they must be are set by the sections right after this one:
• Up to six switches or circuit breakers may serve as the disconnect, in a single enclosure or a group of separate enclosures (225.33)
• The disconnects are grouped together, and each one is marked to show exactly what it disconnects (225.34)
• A feeder disconnect serving a one-family dwelling is rated at least 100 A (225.39(C)); the floor for all others is 60 A (225.39(D))
• The disconnect must be suitable for use as service equipment where it is applied under 250.32(B)(1) Exception No. 1 (225.36)
sections.on_the_job:
Mount and label the disconnect at rough-in, not at final. If the feeder feeds a subpanel inside the building, confirm which device is the building disconnect and that it is grouped and marked as such. On a detached garage fed from a house panel in Marion Oaks, the grouped disconnects on the garage wall are the building disconnect — the breaker back in the house is not.

Count the disconnects before you set the gear: if the design needs a seventh throw, the design changes — one larger disconnecting means or a single main — not a seventh handle in a second can across the room.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A fire or a fault in a detached garage cannot wait for a run back to the house panel. The building disconnect puts one obvious place, at the building itself, where every ungrounded conductor can be opened at once. Grouping and marking carry the same idea: under stress, nobody should have to guess which handle kills what, or hunt for a handle in another room.
inspection_fails: No disconnect at the detached building — power can only be killed back at the main house.
Seven switches at the building; the 225.33 limit is six.
Disconnects split up — one by the door, another across the room — instead of grouped (225.34).
Disconnect not marked to show what it disconnects.
60 A feeder disconnect serving a one-family dwelling; the 225.39(C) floor is 100 A.
sections.exam_trap: The citation swap: 100 A for a one-family dwelling is 225.39(C), not (D) — 225.39(D) is 'all others' at 60 A. The field trap is counting the breaker in the main house as the building disconnect; 225.31 puts the disconnecting means at the building being supplied.

sections.title: Where the separate building's disconnect must be
sections.plain_explanation: The disconnecting means for a feeder or branch circuit supplying a separate building goes in a readily accessible location either outside the building or inside, nearest the point where the conductors enter. 'Nearest the point of entrance' is the load-bearing phrase: feeder conductors inside the building are ahead of the building's own disconnect until they reach it, so the run from the entry point to the disconnect is kept as short as the building allows. Exceptions cover large multibuilding industrial or institutional sites under single management with documented safe switching, and poles or towers used as lighting standards, among others; read the listed exceptions in the printed text before relying on one. Fire pumps are an additional-supply permission under 225.30, not a 225.32 location exception. For this section, the 230.6 rules decide when conductors are considered outside the building.
sections.on_the_job: On a detached garage or casita, plan the panel or disconnect at the wall where the feeder enters — not across the building because the layout was prettier. If the feeder enters underground on the far side from the planned panel, that is a redesign conversation before the trench, not after.
sections.figure_idea: Detached building plan: feeder entering at the near wall with the disconnect right at the entry, and a crossed-out long interior run to a far panel.

sections.why_it_exists: Conductors ahead of the building's disconnect have no local shutoff. If a fault starts in that inside run, the only protection is the feeder breaker back in the main building — and nobody in the garage can kill it. Keeping the disconnect at the point of entrance keeps the unprotected inside run as short as possible and puts the shutoff where a person entering the building can reach it.
inspection_fails: Disconnect or panel placed across the building from the feeder entry, with a long conductor run inside ahead of it.
Disconnect inside the building but not readily accessible — behind stored material or in a locked room.

No disconnecting means at the separate building at all — the crew is relying on the breaker in the main house.
Industrial or institutional campus exception claimed for an ordinary detached garage.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the separate building like a subpanel in the same building and landing the disconnect wherever it fits the layout. 225.32 wants it outside, or inside nearest the point of entrance. The second trap: citing a fire pump as a 225.32 location exception. A fire pump is an additional-supply permission under 225.30, not an exception to this section.

sections.title: Services — where utility power enters
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 230 governs the service: the conductors and equipment that bring utility power to the building and end at the service disconnect. It answers the questions every job starts with:
• How many services may a building have, and how do the conductors arrive — by overhead drop or by underground lateral?
• How are service-entrance conductors wired and sized, including the minimum size for a dwelling service?
• Where does the service disconnect go, how many disconnects may there be, and how are they grouped?
• What else must the service include: barriers in service equipment, surge protection (230.67), and for one- and two-family dwellings an outdoor emergency disconnect (230.85)?
The meter and panel layout a builder notices most is decided here and in Article 250, which covers the grounding and bonding that land at the same point. Article 230 ends at the service disconnect; everything beyond it is a feeder or a branch circuit.
sections.on_the_job: Plan the service on a new Marion Oaks house as one assembly at rough-in, not five separate decisions: the utility drop or lateral and its clearances; the Siemens meter-main outside (S-02), which is both the service disconnect and the 230.85 emergency disconnect; the surge protective device the 2020 code requires on dwelling services (230.67); the grounding electrode system of Article 250 landed at the same point; and the indoor panel directly behind the meter where the house allows (S-09), fed as a feeder panel with neutrals and grounds separated. Finding one piece missing at final — an unlabeled emergency disconnect, no SPD — is a failed inspection and a second trip.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside, panel inside directly behind it, where the house allows. S-02: new service gear is Siemens.

nec2023_change.change: Type TC-ER cable can now carry underground service conductors, but only when the cable is identified for both direct burial and service-entrance use. Underground service conductors can now run in Type TC-ER cable (230.30(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.30 TC-ER cable for underground services

nec2023_change.change: Type TC-ER cable still works for service-entrance conductors, but only cable identified for service-entrance use counts now. Ordinary TC-ER, allowed in 2020, no longer qualifies. Only TC-ER that carries a service-entrance identification can be used for service-entrance conductors (230.43(20)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.43 TC-ER for service-entrance conductors

nec2023_change.change: The barrier rule in service equipment now plainly covers the parts that stay energized with the service disconnect open, so a worker on the load side can't brush live line terminals. Barriers have to guard energized, uninsulated, ungrounded busbars and terminals while the service disconnect is open (230.62(C)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.62 Service equipment barriers

nec2023_change.change: Underground boxes and handhole enclosures joined the list. Other conductors can't share a service raceway, service cable, underground box or handhole with the service conductors. Feeders and branch circuits can't ride in the same underground box or handhole enclosure as the service conductors.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.7 Service conductors kept separate

nec2023_change.change: The section of a multi-section switchboard or switchgear lineup that holds the neutral disconnect has to be marked again. The 2020 edition had left that marking rule out. Multi-section switchboards and switchgear can put the neutral disconnect in any one section, and that section now has to be marked.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.75 Neutral disconnect in service gear

nec2023_change.change: Underground service raceways entering a building still get sealed, and in 2023 the seal also has to meet 300.7(A) for temperature differences, not just 300.5(G). The seal now has to satisfy 300.7(A) too, which targets warm air moving into a cold section of raceway and condensing.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.8 Service raceway seals

sections.why_it_exists: The service is the one part of the system with no building-side breaker ahead of it: a fault in service conductors burns until something on the utility side gives way. That is why this article is strict about where the conductors run, how quickly a person can reach the disconnect, how many throws it takes to kill the service, and what stands between a worker and the parts that stay energized with the disconnect open.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calling everything from the utility pole 'the service.' Service conductors end at the service disconnect: the conductors between an outdoor meter-main and the indoor panel are feeders, and feeder rules for separating neutrals and grounds apply to them. Second trap: the disconnect count. The rule is a maximum of six grouped disconnects at one location (230.71) — not one disconnect per space, scattered around the building.
inspection_fails: No surge protective device on a new dwelling service (230.67).
Emergency disconnect missing, unlabeled, or not in a readily accessible outdoor location (230.85).
Service disconnects scattered around the building instead of grouped, or more than six throws to disconnect the service (230.71).
Feeder or branch-circuit conductors sharing a raceway, underground box or handhole with service conductors (230.7).
Underground service raceway entering the building left unsealed (230.8).

page_quiz.question: Article 230's rules for service conductors end at:
page_quiz.explain_plain: The service is the conductors and equipment up to the service disconnecting means; beyond it, conductors are feeders or branch circuits.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 230.71 allows not more than six switches or circuit breakers, grouped, as the service disconnecting means.

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 230.30: Type TC-ER cable can now carry underground service conductors, but only when the cable is identified for both direct burial and service-entrance use. Underground service conductors can now run in Type TC-ER cable (230.30(B)).
• 230.43: Type TC-ER cable still works for service-entrance conductors, but only cable identified for service-entrance use counts now. Ordinary TC-ER, allowed in 2020, no longer qualifies. Only TC-ER that carries a service-entrance identification can be used for service-entrance conductors (230.43(20)).
• 230.62: The barrier rule in service equipment now plainly covers the parts that stay energized with the service disconnect open, so a worker on the load side can't brush live line terminals. Barriers have to guard energized, uninsulated, ungrounded busbars and terminals while the service disconnect is open (230.62(C)).
• 230.7: Underground boxes and handhole enclosures joined the list. Other conductors can't share a service raceway, service cable, underground box or handhole with the service conductors. Feeders and branch circuits can't ride in the same underground box or handhole enclosure as the service conductors.
• 230.75: The section of a multi-section switchboard or switchgear lineup that holds the neutral disconnect has to be marked again. The 2020 edition had left that marking rule out. Multi-section switchboards and switchgear can put the neutral disconnect in any one section, and that section now has to be marked.
• 230.8: Underground service raceways entering a building still get sealed, and in 2023 the seal also has to meet 300.7(A) for temperature differences, not just 300.5(G). The seal now has to satisfy 300.7(A) too, which targets warm air moving into a cold section of raceway and condensing.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

sections.title: Clearances for service conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Service conductors that run where people can reach them need clearance from the building openings they pass. This section sets the clearance from windows, doors, and similar features; the vertical clearances over roofs, yards, driveways, and streets are a separate set of numbers in 230.24, covered on its own page.
• At least 3 ft from windows that are designed to be opened, doors, porches, balconies, fire escapes, and similar features
• Conductors run above the top level of a window are the stated exception to that 3 ft clearance
• The 3 ft rule applies to open conductors and to multiconductor cable without an overall outer jacket — jacketed SE cable is not subject to it
• Conductors above platforms and similar areas need the 10 ft vertical clearance of 230.24(B) (230.9(B))
• Overhead service conductors may not be installed beneath openings through which materials may be moved, and may not obstruct those openings (230.9(C))
Underground services and other arrangements are handled by their own parts of Article 230 and by the Article 300 burial rules.
sections.on_the_job: Check the drop against the finished building, not the framing: a window that will open, a porch roof, and a balcony added on a plan revision all change the clearance picture. On a two-story Sharma house the drop often passes the second-floor bath window — measure the 3 ft from the window as it will operate, and where the drop crosses over the porch platform, hold the 10 ft vertical clearance of 230.24(B) as well.
sections.florida_note: The utility's own service standards also apply in Florida and may be stricter at the pole and weatherhead; the AHJ and the serving utility both have a say at the service.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A service drop has no building overcurrent protection ahead of it, and it hangs where ladders, window washers, and kids on a balcony can reach it. The 3 ft standoff keeps an energized conductor out of arm's reach of an opening, and the platform rule keeps it well over head height where people stand.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is applying the 3 ft to every window: the rule names windows designed to be opened, and conductors above the top level of a window are excepted. The reverse trap: assuming jacketed SE cable needs the 3 ft. It does not — the rule reaches open conductors and multiconductor cable without an overall outer jacket.
inspection_fails: Drop passing within 3 ft of a second-story window that opens, after a plan revision changed the window package.
Service conductors run beneath a material-handling opening, where they can be struck or block the opening (230.9(C)).
Conductors over a porch or balcony platform below the 10 ft vertical clearance of 230.24(B).
Open conductors run within reach of a fire escape landing.

sections.title: Overhead service conductors — clearance heights
sections.plain_explanation:
These are the heights overhead service conductors and drops must keep, measured to the lowest point of the span, including the drip loop:
• Above a roof — 8 ft, kept for at least 3 ft in all directions from the edge of the roof
• Above a roof with a slope of 4 in 12 or steeper, where the voltage between conductors does not exceed 300 V — 3 ft is permitted
• Over a roof overhang only — as low as 18 in, where not more than 6 ft of conductor passes over not more than 4 ft of overhang and the conductors terminate in a through-the-roof raceway or approved support (the mast case)
The mast is built to whichever number the span actually crosses — the utility's own service standards may require more. Section 230.24(B) then sets the ground clearances by voltage:
• 10 ft — at the service entrance, at the lowest point of the drip loop, and over pedestrian-only areas; only for conductors supported on and cabled with a grounded bare messenger and not over 150 V to ground
• 12 ft — residential property and driveways, and commercial areas not subject to truck traffic, not over 300 V to ground
• 15 ft — those 12 ft areas where the voltage exceeds 300 V to ground
• 18 ft — public streets, alleys, roads, parking areas subject to truck traffic, driveways on other than residential property, and other land traversed by vehicles (cultivated, grazing, forest, orchard)
• 24.5 ft — over track rails
• Exception No. 4: the 3 ft-beyond-the-edge requirement does not apply to the final span attached to the side of the building
• Exception No. 5: 3 ft is permitted where the voltage between conductors does not exceed 300 V and the roof area is guarded or isolated
sections.on_the_job: Set the mast height from the span, not from habit: measure the route, find the highest clearance it crosses, add sag, and that is the weatherhead height. A drop that clears the roof by 8 ft but sags to 11 ft over the driveway fails the driveway number.
sections.figure_idea: House elevation with a service mast: 8 ft dimensioned above the roof, 3 ft at the steep-slope case, and 12 ft dimensioned where the drop crosses the driveway.

nec2023_change.change: Service conductors running over a roof must now clear it by 8 ft 6 in, not 8 ft. Overhead feeders already used that number. The minimum height from the roof surface up to overhead service conductors is now 8 ft 6 in instead of 8 ft (230.24(A)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.24 Service conductor clearance over roofs

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 230.24: Service conductors running over a roof must now clear it by 8 ft 6 in, not 8 ft. Overhead feeders already used that number. The minimum height from the roof surface up to overhead service conductors is now 8 ft 6 in instead of 8 ft (230.24(A)).

sections.why_it_exists: The drop is bare, unfused conductor. Nothing trips if a ladder or a delivery truck reaches it — clearance is the whole protection. The numbers rise with what moves underneath: a pedestrian gets 10 ft, a residential driveway 12 ft, and a truck route 18 ft.
inspection_fails: Drop sags to 11 ft over the residential driveway — 12 ft is required at the lowest point.
Roof clearance of 8 ft held only at the mast, not for 3 ft in all directions from the roof edge.
Overhang case stretched: more than 6 ft of conductor over more than 4 ft of overhang at 18 in.
Lowest point of the drip loop under 10 ft at the service entrance.
18 ft truck-traffic clearance missed where the drop crosses a commercial drive.
sections.exam_trap: Measuring at the mast instead of at the lowest point of the span. Sag and the drip loop count — a drop legal at the weatherhead can fail over the driveway. Second trap: taking the 3 ft roof number on a low-slope roof; it needs a 4 in 12 slope or steeper and no more than 300 V between conductors.

sections.title: Service masts — what may ride on the mast
sections.plain_explanation: Where a mast is used to support overhead service conductors, the mast itself is part of the service. Only power service-drop or overhead service conductors may be attached to it — no other conductors, and no antennas or other equipment that is not part of the service. The mast has to be strong enough for the strain the utility's drop puts on it, or be braced or guyed, and the fittings where conductors pass through or terminate are listed service fittings (the weatherhead and drip loop are on the 230.54 page). A mast that also carries a yard-light feed or a cable TV drop is a violation you can see from the street. 230.28(A): hubs used with a conduit service mast must be identified for use with service-entrance equipment. 230.28(B): service-drop or overhead service conductors may not be attached to the mast between the weatherhead (or end of the conduit) and a coupling where the coupling is above the last conduit support or above the building.
sections.on_the_job: Check the mast before the utility arrives: listed weatherhead, hub wrench-tight, guys where the span is long, and nothing else clamped to the pipe. Confirm the utility's attachment requirements at rough-in — masts through or over the roof carry height and bracing rules in the serving utility's standards as well.
sections.figure_idea: Service mast elevation: weatherhead, drip loop, and guys, with a red X over a TV antenna and a yard-light cable clamped to the same mast.
sections.florida_note: Florida utilities publish their own service standards (attachment heights, mast specifications, meter positions). The NEC sets the floor; the serving utility's book can add to it, and the utility connects last — build to both.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The mast is the anchor point for the utility's drop, and the drop pulls on it every day — more in a Florida storm. Anything else clamped to the mast adds wind load and strain the mast was never sized for, and puts foreign wiring in the one place reserved for the service. If the mast bends or pulls loose, it takes live, unfused service conductors down with it.
inspection_fails: Cable TV drop or antenna clamped to the service mast.
Yard-light feed run up the mast with the service conductors.
Service drop attached between the weatherhead and a coupling above the last conduit support (230.28(B)).
Mast hub not identified for use with service-entrance equipment (230.28(A)).
Mast left unbraced on a long span — bent or pulling away from the wall.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the TV drop can ride the mast if it is bonded to it.' No — bonding does not make it a service conductor. Only power service-drop or overhead service conductors may be attached to the mast; antennas and every other conductor stay off, bonded or not.

sections.title: Minimum size and rating of service-entrance conductors
sections.plain_explanation: Service-entrance conductors are sized for the calculated load from Article 220 — the calculation, not the size of the panel that was ordered, sets the floor. The conductor ampacity has to carry the load and coordinate with the service overcurrent protection. For a one-family dwelling the service disconnect itself may not be smaller than 100A (that rating rule is on the 230.79(C) page), and dwelling services and whole-load feeders may use the 83 percent sizing rule covered in Chapter 3 at 310.12 — for services rated 100A through 400A that carry the entire dwelling load. A 200A panel fed by conductors sized for 100A of calculated load is not a 200A service.
sections.on_the_job: Use the optional-method worked example in this book (220.82): an 1,800 sq ft house whose calculation lands at 25,160 VA — about 105 A at 240 V. The 100A floor in 230.79(C) does not save a 100A service here: the conductors and the disconnect must carry 105 A, so the service is built at the next size up. On paper, the same house with a 200A panel and conductors sized for only 100A of load would still be a 100A-class installation wearing a 200A label. Do the Article 220 math before the service gear is ordered, and keep the worksheet in the job file — if the calculated load lands close to the next standard size, that is a conversation for the office, not a field decision to round the conductors down.
sections.figure_idea: Flow line: Article 220 load → conductor ampacity (or 310.12 for a dwelling) → service disconnect rating → panel, with 'panel size alone' crossed out as a starting point.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Conductors sized below the real load run hot for the life of the house, and the failure shows up years later as cooked insulation inside a wall or a meter base. Sizing from the calculation — not from the panel label or the sales sheet — is what keeps the service honest: the wire, the disconnect, and the load all tell the same story when an inspector or the next electrician opens it up.
inspection_fails: Service conductors sized to the panel label instead of the Article 220 calculated load.
200A panel installed on conductors sized for a 100A load and passed off as a 200A service.
Table 310.12 used for a feeder that carries only part of the dwelling load.
Service disconnect rated below the calculated load because '100A is the house minimum.'
sections.exam_trap: The wrong answer sizes the conductors to the panel: '200A panel, so 200A conductors' — or worse, '200A panel, conductors whatever was on the truck.' 230.42 runs the other way: the Article 220 calculation sets the conductor size, the disconnect must be at least the calculated load, and the panel rating is just the last number in the chain.

sections.title: Overhead service connections — attachment and drip loop
sections.plain_explanation: Where an overhead drop lands, three things have to be right at the top of the service. The point of attachment is located so the clearances on the 230.24 and 230.9 pages can actually be met, and the service head (weatherhead) sits at or above the point of attachment wherever practicable, so water runs away from the raceway instead of into it. The conductors form a drip loop below the weatherhead: each conductor loops down and back up, so rain drips off the bottom of the loop instead of following the wire into the head. Service heads must have conductors of different potential brought out through separately bushed openings (230.54(E)), and splices in service conductors are made only by the methods 230.46 allows. Where it is impracticable to put the service head above the point of attachment, it must be within 24 in. of the point of attachment (230.54(C) exception). Drip loops and service-entrance conductors must be arranged so water will not enter the raceway or equipment (230.54(F), (G)).
sections.on_the_job: Form the drip loop long enough to actually drip — a tight little kink at the head is not a loop. Leave the utility the working tails at the length its standards call for, and do not tape or splice anything at the weatherhead that the utility will have to undo. On a Sharma overhead service, set the attachment so the clearances work, land the head above the attachment, and form each loop below the head before the utility makes its connections. If the wall layout forces the head below the attachment point, keep it within 24 in. — and expect the inspector to measure it.
sections.figure_idea: Weatherhead detail: attachment point, head above it, drip loop hanging below with a droplet falling from the bottom of the loop.
sections.florida_note: The serving Florida utility's standards set the tail length it wants at the weatherhead and the attachment hardware it accepts; confirm both before the drop is scheduled.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Rain is the enemy at the top of a service. Water that follows a conductor into the weatherhead runs down inside the raceway, corrodes lugs and conductor ends, and can reach the meter and the panel. Florida storms drive rain sideways, so the geometry has to shed water by gravity: head high, loop low, drip off the bottom. The separately bushed openings also keep conductors of different potential from chafing on one shared edge.
inspection_fails: Weatherhead below the point of attachment with no impracticable condition — and more than 24 in. away from it.
No drip loop: conductors run straight into the head, or the loop is taped flat against the mast.
Conductors of different potential brought out of the service head through one shared opening instead of separately bushed openings (230.54(E)).
Splice in the service conductors at the weatherhead made by a method 230.46 does not allow.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: the weatherhead can sit below the point of attachment as long as the splices are well taped. It cannot. Below the attachment is allowed only where putting the head above is impracticable — and then the head must be within 24 in. of the attachment point. Tape is not a drip loop either: the loop has to hang below the head so water drips off its bottom.

sections.title: Surge protection on the service
sections.plain_explanation: New in the 2020 edition, this section requires surge protection when a service supplies a dwelling unit: a listed Type 1 or Type 2 surge protective device (SPD), installed in the service equipment or in an enclosure right next to it. The rule also bites on replacement: when the service equipment of a dwelling is replaced, the new equipment needs the SPD too. The device clamps surges arriving on the service conductors and shunts them to ground before they can spread through the house wiring. It is not a lightning protection system, and it is not a substitute for point-of-use protection on sensitive gear.
sections.on_the_job: On every new Sharma house service — a 200 A Siemens meter-main in Marion Oaks, say — the SPD is on the material list with the service gear (S-02), integral to the meter-main or in its own enclosure beside it, and drawn on the service sketch before rough-in. Confirm the same on every service change. The miss that fails inspections is the storm repair: a damaged meter-main swapped like-for-like with no SPD, because "we only replaced what was there." Section 230.67 counts that replacement as a trigger. A surge device left in the truck is a failed item.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: new gear is Siemens, so the SPD choice follows the Siemens service equipment on Sharma jobs.
sections.figure_idea: A panel with an integral surge device shown beside the main breaker and a short lead connection drawn in.

nec2023_change.change: SPD rule spread to feeders: new 215.18 and 225.42 require a Type 1 or Type 2 SPD (10 kA In minimum) where a feeder supplies a dwelling unit, dormitory unit, hotel/motel guest room or nursing-home sleeping area. Article 242 itself is not new in 2023 (it was new in 2020); 2023 adds 242.2 (SPDs and surge arresters may not be reconditioned).
nec2023_change.source: Eaton 2023 NEC surge page; Carosella 2023 NEC workbook (215.18, 225.42, 230.67, 242.2)

nec2023_change.change: Surge protection at the service now reaches dorm units, hotel and motel guest suites and rooms, and nursing home patient sleeping areas. The device itself now needs a 10 kA minimum nominal discharge current rating. Dorm units and the guest rooms and suites of hotels and motels joined dwelling units: their services now need a surge-protective device (SPD).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.67 Surge protection beyond dwellings

nec2023_change.change: Starting in 2023, every surge-protective device (SPD) has to show whether it is still working, so anyone can tell when the protection is gone. Every SPD now needs a way to show it is working properly (242.9).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 242.9 SPD status indicator

sections.why_it_exists: Florida is lightning country, but most damaging surges never come from a direct strike. Utility switching and strikes blocks away push a voltage spike down the service drop, and that spike hunts for the weakest board in the house — the air handler control board, the refrigerator board, the TV. An SPD at the service meets the surge at the door and dumps its energy to ground while it is still small enough to handle, instead of letting it divide among every electronic device in the home.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: a plug-in surge strip at the TV satisfies 230.67. It does not — a strip is a Type 3 point-of-use device, and the rule wants a listed Type 1 or Type 2 SPD at the service equipment. Second trap: "SPDs are only for new construction." Replacing the service equipment on an existing dwelling triggers the same rule.
inspection_fails: New dwelling service with no SPD installed at all — the 2020 rule is still missed on site.
Service equipment replaced after storm damage, like-for-like, with no SPD added.
A Type 3 plug-in strip offered as the service surge protective device.
SPD landed in a downstream subpanel instead of in or next to the service equipment.
SPD in place but dead — status indicator dark — and left in service.

sections.title: Where the service disconnect goes
sections.plain_explanation:
The service disconnecting means has to be:
• Readily accessible
• Outside the building, or inside nearest the point where the service conductors enter (230.70(A)(1))
That is the list of places it may go, subject to the 2020 wording and to what the AHJ accepts for conductor length inside. Every occupant also needs access to disconnecting means for their own space in the occupancies the section covers. The disconnect is what everything downstream is judged from — it is where the service ends and feeders and branch circuits begin.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma's standard is S-09, the back-to-back layout: meter on the outside wall, panel directly behind it, so the service conductors inside are measured in inches, not feet. Decide the disconnect location with the inspector's local practice in mind before the service is built, especially on a service change where an older inside location is being reused — an AHJ who wants an outside disconnect will not accept 'it was already there.' Keep the path to it clear and the location marked. On a house, do not confuse this with the 230.85 emergency disconnect: that is a separate outdoor switch for first responders, not the service disconnect itself.
sections.sharma_note: S-09's back-to-back layout puts the panel directly behind the meter, which keeps service conductors inside the building to the shortest practical run.
sections.florida_note: Florida AHJs differ on how much service conductor they accept inside a building before the disconnect. Confirm the local position on a service layout that is not the standard back-to-back arrangement.
sections.why_it_exists: The conductors ahead of the disconnect have no overcurrent protection on the premises side — only the utility's fuse, far away and slow. Every foot of that unfused conductor inside the building is a fault waiting to burn until the utility lets go. Putting the disconnect outside, or hard against the entry point, keeps the unprotected run as short as possible — and ready access means anyone can kill the building in an emergency.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'The service disconnect may go anywhere inside, as long as it is readily accessible.' Wrong — inside means nearest the point of entrance. A panel at the far end of the house, fed by a long run of unfused conductor through the attic, fails the location rule even though anyone can reach it.
inspection_fails: Service disconnect deep inside the building on a long unfused conductor run, with no AHJ acceptance of the length inside.
Disconnect behind a locked door or blocked by stored material — not readily accessible.
Tenant in a multi-occupancy building cannot reach the disconnecting means for their own space.
Service change rebuilt on the old interior location without confirming the AHJ still accepts it.

sections.title: How many service disconnects, and how they are grouped
sections.plain_explanation:
One disconnect is always fine; this section governs a service built with more than one. The 2020 edition reorganized the multi-disconnect rule: a service may have two to six disconnecting means, grouped together, and 230.71(B) permits four arrangements:
• (1) Separate enclosures for each disconnect
• (2) Panelboards, each with its own main disconnect
• (3) A switchboard with each disconnect in a separate barriered vertical section
• (4) Switchgear or metering centers with each disconnect in its own compartment
The disconnects must be grouped as 230.71(A) requires. A single multi-switch assembly is not automatically wrong — it counts where it fits one of these four arrangements. What 2020 ended is the old habit of landing several unrelated mains loose in one enclosure with no barriers between them.
sections.on_the_job: On a small Sharma commercial service — a 400 A switchboard feeding a plaza unit — three service disconnects sit in three barriered vertical sections of one switchboard, grouped on the same wall, each labeled for the load it kills: arrangement (3). On a duplex, two panelboards side by side, each with its own main, do the same job under arrangement (2). Draw the arrangement and the grouping on the service sketch; if all the disconnects cannot be taken in at one glance, the layout is wrong.

nec2023_change.change: Transfer switches and motor control centers joined the two-to-six disconnect list, separate meter centers got their own item, and older equipment that legally grouped service disconnects in one enclosure gets a pass. New exception: existing service equipment built under an older edition that allowed grouped disconnects can keep up to six in one enclosure, section or compartment.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 230.71 Up to six service disconnects

sections.why_it_exists: Grouping is about the worst day, not the normal one. When a building is burning or a service is faulting, one person has to kill all the power in one place, in seconds, without hunting through rooms. The 2020 separation rules add a second protection: a fault or a fire inside one disconnect section cannot reach across and take the neighboring disconnects — and the whole service — with it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "Up to six disconnects, so six mains loose in one big enclosure is fine." That was the old way. Under 2020, six disconnects pass only inside one of the four arrangements — separate enclosures, panelboards with mains, barriered switchboard sections, or compartmented switchgear and metering centers. The mirror trap — "every disconnect needs its own enclosure" — is also wrong: arrangements (2) through (4) exist precisely so grouped gear can comply.
inspection_fails: Seven service disconnects installed on one service — two too many over the six-disconnect limit.
Disconnects scattered between rooms or between indoors and outdoors, not grouped.
Several mains landed loose in one unbarriered enclosure on a new 2020 installation.
Grouped disconnects with no marking to say which load each one kills.

sections.title: Minimum size for a one-family dwelling service
sections.plain_explanation:
A one-family dwelling service disconnect is rated at least 100 amperes, 3-wire. That is a floor, not a recommendation: the disconnect rating must also be at least the calculated load from Article 220, and the Article 220 calculation governs whenever it comes out higher, which on a modern Florida house with electric range, dryer, water heating, and air conditioning it usually does. The other floors in 230.79 sit around it:
• (A) An installation of a single branch circuit: 15 amperes
• (B) An installation of two 2-wire branch circuits: 30 amperes
• (C) A one-family dwelling: 100 amperes, 3-wire
• (D) All other installations: 60 amperes
Grabbing the (D) 60-ampere floor for a house, or treating the (C) floor as the design size, are the two mistakes this section produces.
sections.on_the_job: Never quote a 100A service because it is the minimum. Run the calculation, and if the result is close to a standard size, say so with the worksheet in hand. On Sharma's new one-family work the standard gear is a 200A Siemens meter-main — not because 230.79(C) asks for 200, but because the Article 220 result on a modern Florida house lands well past the 100A floor. The 100A number is what you check the calculation against, never the answer you start from.
sections.why_it_exists: The service disconnect is the one device that has to carry and interrupt everything the building can draw. A floor under its rating keeps a builder from hanging a whole house on a disconnect sized for a shed, and tying the rating to the Article 220 calculation keeps the disconnect ahead of the real load as houses add air conditioning, cooking and water heating.
inspection_fails: 100A service disconnect installed where the Article 220 calculated load is higher than 100A.
60A disconnect used for a one-family dwelling — the (D) floor applied to a (C) job.
Service quoted and roughed at the 100A minimum with no load calculation on file.
Disconnect rating matched to the old service on a change-out while the panel schedule shows added air conditioning and cooking loads.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap states the rule backwards: 'a one-family dwelling requires a 100-ampere service.' No — 100 amperes, 3-wire is the minimum rating for the service disconnect. When the Article 220 calculation comes out higher, the higher number governs, and a 100A disconnect on a house that calculates past it fails.

tables.caption: The floors in 230.79
tables.note: The rating must also be at least the Article 220 calculated load; the floor never lowers the calculation.

figures.caption: 100 A is the floor for a one-family dwelling; the Article 220 calculation governs above it.

sections.title: What may connect ahead of the service disconnect
sections.plain_explanation:
The line side of the service disconnect is a closed list: only the equipment named in 230.82 may connect ahead of it. The list:
• Cable limiters or other current-limiting devices
• Meter enclosures and meter disconnect switches
• Current-transformer cabinets
• Type 1 surge-protective devices and surge arresters
• Taps that supply only load-management devices
• Circuits for standby power systems, fire pump equipment, and fire and sprinkler alarms — where they are provided with service equipment and installed as service-entrance conductors, under their own articles
• Supply-side interconnections, such as a solar system connected ahead of the main under Article 705
Two items carry their own conditions. A meter disconnect switch must have a short-circuit current rating at least equal to the available fault current, must be able to interrupt the load it serves, and must be field-marked "METER DISCONNECT – NOT SERVICE EQUIPMENT". A supply-side source under Article 705 needs a disconnect suitable for use as service equipment and overcurrent protection per Part VII of that article. The 230.67 dwelling SPD may sit on the line side or the load side of the service disconnect; it is usually a Type 1 or Type 2 device at the service equipment. Anything not on this list waits for the load side.
sections.on_the_job: Solar supply-side taps are the live case on Sharma roofs: the tap hardware, its rating, and where it lands are engineered decisions made before rough-in, with the utility and the AHJ in the loop — never a field improvisation inside a meter can. The same discipline covers the Type 1 SPD in a new Siemens meter-main: it is on the list, so it may land ahead of the main breaker. A convenience receptacle or a doorbell transformer may not — those wait for a load-side breaker.
sections.figure_idea: One-line of a service: utility → meter → allowed line-side items tagged → service disconnect → panel, with a random branch circuit tapped ahead of the main crossed out.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Conductors ahead of the service disconnect have no overcurrent protection from the building — a fault on them burns until the utility's protection clears it or the conductor fails. Keeping the line side to a short list of service-grade equipment keeps those unprotected runs short, enclosed, and limited to gear built for that duty.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the line side like a junction box: a tap for a landscape-lighting transformer or a "temporary" receptacle ahead of the main is not on the list, so it is a violation no matter how small the load. Second trap: a meter disconnect is not service equipment — its marking says so — so the main bonding jumper does not land there.
inspection_fails: PV supply-side tap made with unlisted hardware, or landed ahead of the main without the Article 705 disconnect and overcurrent protection.
Meter disconnect switch with no field marking, or with a short-circuit current rating below the available fault current in the utility letter.
Type 2 SPD connected ahead of the service disconnect — the 230.82 list names Type 1 devices for the line side.
Load-management tap that also feeds general loads instead of only the load-management device.
Branch circuit tapped ahead of the service disconnect "because the panel was full".

sections.title: An outdoor emergency disconnect for dwellings
sections.plain_explanation:
For one- and two-family dwellings, all service conductors must terminate in a disconnecting means in a readily accessible outdoor location. Its short-circuit current rating must be at least the available fault current, and if there is more than one, they are grouped. NEC 2020 allows three kinds, each with its own marking:
• (1) The service disconnect itself, outdoors: EMERGENCY DISCONNECT, SERVICE DISCONNECT
• (2) A meter disconnect installed per 230.82(3): EMERGENCY DISCONNECT, METER DISCONNECT, NOT SERVICE EQUIPMENT
• (3) Another listed disconnect switch or circuit breaker on the supply side of each service disconnect, suitable for use as service equipment: EMERGENCY DISCONNECT, NOT SERVICE EQUIPMENT
Markings must be permanent and durable for the environment (110.21(B)). The service disconnect location rule still applies: readily accessible, outside, or inside nearest the point where the service conductors enter (230.70(A)(1)), and never in a bathroom (230.70(A)(2)).
sections.on_the_job: Sharma's standard new service is an outdoor Siemens meter-main (S-02). Its main breaker is both the service disconnect and the emergency disconnect (Option 1). It carries the main bonding jumper and the GEC, and the label reads EMERGENCY DISCONNECT, SERVICE DISCONNECT. The interior panel is then fed as a feeder panel: four-wire feeder, isolated neutral bar, grounds on their own bar, no bonding screw. Where a builder wants the main inside, use Option 3: a listed outdoor switch marked NOT SERVICE EQUIPMENT, with the indoor service panel nearest the point of entrance. Confirm with the AHJ how much service conductor they accept inside.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: the device is part of the Siemens service gear package on a new Sharma service.
sections.figure_idea: An outdoor meter-main on a house wall with the emergency disconnect handle and its marking highlighted.
sections.florida_note: Florida AHJs differ on how much service conductor they accept inside a building before the disconnect (see 230.70). Confirm the local position whenever the service is not an outdoor meter-main.

sections.why_it_exists: Firefighters need to kill power to a burning house without walking into it. Before 2020 the only disconnect was often an indoor panel in a garage full of smoke. A labeled switch outside at the meter lets the first crew on scene de-energize the house in seconds.

sections.exam_trap: An indoor main panel in the garage and an outdoor meter: can the fire department just pull the meter? Not for 230.85. Pulling a meter is not a disconnecting means; the rule wants a listed disconnect outdoors. sections.title: Overcurrent protection — breakers and fuses
sections.plain_explanation: Article 240 is the protection article: it decides where overcurrent devices go, what standard ratings exist, how conductors are protected, when the next higher rating may be used, how tap conductors work, and where panels may and may not be located. A breaker has two jobs that must not be confused — it protects the conductor, and only through that does it protect the equipment and the building. The standard ratings live in 240.6, the tap rules in 240.21, and the location rules in 240.24: devices readily accessible, the center of the handle grip no higher than 6 ft 7 in, and in dwellings no overcurrent devices in bathrooms or clothes closets. Most of Article 240 that Sharma uses daily is in 240.4 and 240.24.
sections.on_the_job: For every circuit, ask the Article 240 question out loud: what conductor am I protecting, at what ampacity, and which rule lets me use this breaker size? If the answer is a shrug, the circuit is not designed yet. On a Sharma panel swap, that question catches the classics before the inspector does: a breaker that fits the bus but is not listed for the panel (S-03), and the 30 A breaker someone landed on a 12 AWG run to stop nuisance trips — the conductor's cap is 20 A, and the 'fix' removed its protection.
sections.sharma_note: S-03: in an existing Square D panel, use Square D breakers listed for that panel. Brand mixing is not an Article 240 allowance.
sections.figure_idea: A breaker panel with one breaker lifted out, showing its rating marking and the conductor it protects drawn beside it.

nec2023_change.change: When a rule makes one feeder's overcurrent device selectively coordinate with the service device, every other feeder fed directly from that service device now has to coordinate with it too. Once one feeder device must selectively coordinate with the service device, every feeder device fed straight from that service device must coordinate with it (240.11).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.11 Selective coordination of feeders

nec2023_change.change: Branch-circuit breakers and fuses still need at least 5,000 amps of interrupting rating, but that floor moved out of the Article 100 definition and into new 240.16. Any breaker or fuse doing branch-circuit duty must be rated to interrupt 5,000 amps or more (240.16).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.16 Branch-circuit interrupting rating

nec2023_change.change: New in 2023: a fuse reducer, the adapter that lets a smaller fuse sit in clips made for a bigger one, has to be a listed product. Every fuse reducer now has to be listed. A shop-made spacer or an adapter with no listing mark doesn't pass.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.60 Fuse reducers must be listed

nec2023_change.change: Three kinds of protective devices now have to be listed: branch-circuit breakers and fuses, the relays and breakers that provide ground-fault protection of equipment, and GFCIs. Branch-circuit rated breakers and fuses, the kind that can protect services, feeders and branch circuits, have to be listed. Supplementary protectors aren't on this list.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.7 Listing of protective devices

nec2023_change.change: New in 2023: a replacement trip unit has to carry a listing for use in the specific circuit breaker it goes into. Fitting the frame isn't enough. Swapping a breaker's trip unit? The new unit needs a listing that covers that particular breaker, not just a matching shape.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.89 Replacement breaker trip units

nec2023_change.change: The reconditioning requirements located at 240.62 and 240.88 were relocated to Section 240.2 in the 2023 NEC. Ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) and ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCI) were added to the list of equipment that shall not be reconditioned.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 240.2 Reconditioned Equipment

sections.why_it_exists: Overcurrent is any current beyond what the conductor can carry — an overload that cooks it slowly, or a short circuit or ground fault that delivers thousands of amps in a cycle. Without a device sized and placed by this article, the conductor itself becomes the protection, and it protects by burning. Article 240 puts a listed, rated device between the fault and the fire.
sections.exam_trap: The wrong answer is that the breaker protects the equipment plugged into the receptacle — the toaster, the TV, the appliance. It does not. The breaker protects the conductor; equipment is protected only through the conductor, or by its own article and nameplate. Picking the equipment answer is how a 30 A breaker ends up 'protecting' a 12 AWG circuit.
inspection_fails: Breaker that fits the panel but is not listed for it — brand mixing (S-03).
Overcurrent devices installed in a dwelling bathroom or a clothes closet.
Center of the operating handle higher than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or platform.
Breaker upsized beyond the conductor's ampacity to stop nuisance tripping.

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 240.11: When a rule makes one feeder's overcurrent device selectively coordinate with the service device, every other feeder fed directly from that service device now has to coordinate with it too. Once one feeder device must selectively coordinate with the service device, every feeder device fed straight from that service device must coordinate with it (240.11).
• 240.16: Branch-circuit breakers and fuses still need at least 5,000 amps of interrupting rating, but that floor moved out of the Article 100 definition and into new 240.16. Any breaker or fuse doing branch-circuit duty must be rated to interrupt 5,000 amps or more (240.16).
• 240.60: New in 2023: a fuse reducer, the adapter that lets a smaller fuse sit in clips made for a bigger one, has to be a listed product. Every fuse reducer now has to be listed. A shop-made spacer or an adapter with no listing mark doesn't pass.
• 240.7: Three kinds of protective devices now have to be listed: branch-circuit breakers and fuses, the relays and breakers that provide ground-fault protection of equipment, and GFCIs. Branch-circuit rated breakers and fuses, the kind that can protect services, feeders and branch circuits, have to be listed. Supplementary protectors aren't on this list.
• 240.89: New in 2023: a replacement trip unit has to carry a listing for use in the specific circuit breaker it goes into. Fitting the frame isn't enough. Swapping a breaker's trip unit? The new unit needs a listing that covers that particular breaker, not just a matching shape.
• 240.2: The reconditioning requirements located at 240.62 and 240.88 were relocated to Section 240.2 in the 2023 NEC. Ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) and ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCI) were added to the list of equipment that shall not be reconditioned.

sections.title: Protecting a conductor at its ampacity
sections.plain_explanation:
The starting rule of Article 240 is simple: a conductor is protected against overcurrent at its ampacity. Ampacity comes from Table 310.16, after the correction and adjustment factors of 310.15 — not from the size of breaker that happens to be on the truck. This section then refines the rule:
• Specific equipment plays by its own article. Motors, air conditioning, welders and transformers are sized and protected under their own rules and nameplates, and those rules win over the general rule here.
• Next size up (240.4(B)). Where an ampacity does not land on a standard rating, the next higher standard device may be used — only when all of that subsection's conditions are met, and never above 800 A.
• Small conductors (240.4(D)). 14, 12 and 10 AWG conductors carry hard caps, whatever the ampacity table says.
• Over 800 A (240.4(C)). There is no rounding up at all: the conductor ampacity must be at least equal to the rating of the device.
The two allowances Sharma uses most — rounding up to the next standard rating in limited conditions, and the small-conductor caps — are covered on the next two pages.
sections.on_the_job: When equipment has a nameplate that states its own maximum protection, follow that equipment article and the nameplate — the general rule here is not permission to upsize. Write the special-case citation in the job file when you use one. Worked example: a feeder in 4 AWG copper has a 75 °C ampacity of 85 A (Table 310.16). No standard breaker is 85 A, so a 90 A breaker is allowed under 240.4(B) — the run is a feeder, not a multioutlet receptacle branch circuit, and it is well under 800 A. Run the same trick on a 12 AWG branch circuit and it fails: the table gives 25 A at 75 °C, but 240.4(D) caps 12 AWG copper at 20 A.
sections.sharma_note: S-10 governs the wire this protection is matched to at Sharma: copper by default, CCA one size up, rated in the aluminum column.

nec2023_change.change: Three additions: 14 AWG copper-clad aluminum is capped at 10 amps, adjustable-trip breakers with restricted settings get the next-size-up allowance, and 310.12 sizing for dwelling services and feeders carries over to the breaker. New 240.4(H): a dwelling service or feeder sized with 310.12 can be protected at that full rating, like a 200-amp breaker on 2/0 copper.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.4 Conductor overcurrent protection

sections.why_it_exists: A breaker is the conductor's bodyguard. If the device is bigger than the ampacity, the conductor becomes the fuse: it overheats inside a wall or above a ceiling, cooks its insulation, and starts a fire at a current the breaker sees as normal load. Matching protection to ampacity keeps the weakest link a device that is designed to open — not the wire.
sections.exam_trap: The exam shows a 12 AWG copper conductor, points at the 25 A value in the 75 °C column of Table 310.16, and offers a 25 A breaker. It is wrong: 240.4(D) caps 12 AWG copper at 20 A no matter what the table says. The table gives ampacity; this section decides the protection.
inspection_fails: 30 A breaker landed on a 12 AWG branch circuit 'because it kept tripping' — the cap is 20 A (240.4(D)).
Next-size-up allowance used on a multioutlet branch circuit feeding receptacles — 240.4(B) is not available there.
Condenser breaker upsized past the nameplate maximum overcurrent protection.
Feeder protected above its ampacity with none of the 240.4(B) conditions documented.

sections.title: When the next higher breaker size may be used
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a conductor's ampacity does not land on a standard rating, the next higher standard overcurrent device may be used only when the conditions in this subsection are all met. It is an allowance with fences, not a general right to round up. The existing lookup item works the common examples.

The three conditions:
• (1) The conductors are not part of a branch circuit supplying more than one receptacle for cord-and-plug-connected portable loads
• (2) The conductor ampacity does not correspond to a standard fuse or circuit-breaker rating (breakers without overload-trip adjustment above their rating)
• (3) The next higher standard rating selected does not exceed 800A
There is no separate 'ampacity does not exceed 800A' test in the rule. Past 800A there is no rounding up: under 240.4(C) the conductor ampacity must be at least equal to the device rating.
sections.on_the_job:
State all three conditions when you use this allowance on a feeder or an equipment circuit. If the circuit feeds receptacles on a multi-outlet branch circuit, stop — the allowance is not available.

Worked example: a small commercial feeder in Orlando. After the load calculation and derating, the conductors land at 187A ampacity, which is not a standard rating. The circuit is a feeder, not a multi-outlet receptacle branch circuit, and the next standard size up is 200A — well under 800A. All three conditions are met, so a 200A breaker may protect those conductors. Write the three conditions on the calc sheet; if one of them fails, the wire gets bigger instead.

nec2023_change.change: Added adjustable trip overcurrent protective devices as being permitted to have an ampacity value set that does not exceed the next higher standard overcurrent protection device ampacity value [per Table 240.6(A)] above the ampacity of the conductors being protected.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 240.4(B) Overcurrent Devices Rated 800 Amperes or Less

sections.why_it_exists: Conductors are protected at their ampacity, but standard breaker sizes come in steps, and a calculated ampacity often lands between two steps. For feeders and equipment circuits the Code allows one fenced step up to the next standard size. The fences matter: on a multi-outlet receptacle circuit, portable loads can be plugged in until the breaker itself is the only limit, so no round-up is allowed there — and past 800A the fault energy is so large that the conductor must meet the device rating outright.
inspection_fails: Next higher breaker size used on a multi-outlet receptacle branch circuit.
Breaker rounded up where the conductor ampacity already matched a standard rating.
Round-up used above 800A — 240.4(C) requires ampacity at least equal to the device rating.
Feeder protected one size up with no load calculation on file showing the conductor ampacity.
sections.exam_trap: The classic trap: 'the conductor ampacity must not exceed 800A.' There is no such test in the rule — the 800A cap is on the next higher standard rating you select. Second trap: reaching for the round-up on a multi-outlet receptacle branch circuit, where it is never available.

sections.title: The small-conductor caps
sections.plain_explanation:
Whatever the ampacity table allows at a higher temperature rating, this subsection caps overcurrent protection for small conductors:
• 14 AWG copper — 15 A
• 12 AWG copper — 20 A
• 10 AWG copper — 30 A
• 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum — 15 A
• 10 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum — 25 A
In the 2020 list, 14 AWG aluminum and CCA have no entry at all: 14 AWG CCA is not a 15 A conductor by analogy with copper, and it does not go in on a 2020 permit. (NEC 2023 gives it a limit of its own — see the 2020 vs 2023 box.) Specific equipment articles can direct otherwise for their own equipment, but for general branch wiring these caps are the numbers that decide the breaker. They are also why a 12 AWG conductor on a 25 A breaker fails inspection even when a table column seems to allow the ampacity: Table 310.16 rates 12 AWG THHN at 30 A in the 90 °C column, and the cap still says 20 A.
sections.on_the_job: Memorize the copper row and the aluminum/CCA row separately. On a Marion Oaks house wired in CCA, the rolls follow the breaker, not the copper habit: a 15 A circuit is pulled in 12 AWG CCA and a 20 A circuit in 10 AWG CCA (S-10). Check the roll before it is pulled, not at the panel — finding 12 AWG CCA landed on a 20 A breaker at trim means the run comes out and gets pulled again. On copper the check is one glance at the schedule: 14 AWG never sits above a 15 A breaker and 12 AWG never above a 20 A breaker, whatever the insulation is rated.
sections.sharma_note: S-10 is this rule as Sharma practice: copper 14 on 15A and 12 on 20A; CCA one size up, 12 on 15A and 10 on 20A, with terminations marked for the conductor and no backstabbing.
sections.figure_idea: A three-row chart graphic: wire size, copper cap, aluminum/CCA cap, with the CCA row highlighted.

sections.why_it_exists: Small conductors are the ones that get bundled together, buried in insulation and run the longest distances in a house. The higher table columns assume conditions a finished wall does not give them. The caps build the margin back in at the one place it can be enforced — the breaker — so an overloaded or miswired circuit opens the breaker before the conductor cooks its insulation inside the wall.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer reads the 90 °C column: '12 AWG THHN is good for 30 A, so a 30 A breaker.' 240.4(D) caps it at 20 A, and that cap is the answer. The mirror trap runs by metal: 12 AWG CCA is not a 20 A conductor — aluminum and CCA read one line lower, at 15 A. And on a 2020 question, 14 AWG CCA has no cap in the list at all; the 10 A limit is a 2023 answer, not a 2020 one.

sections.title: Standard ratings for breakers and fuses
sections.plain_explanation:
Overcurrent devices come in standard ampere ratings, and this section lists them — the familiar steps from small branch ratings through the large service ratings, plus the additional standard ratings it names for fuses. Nonstandard ratings exist only in the limited cases the Code allows. A calculation that lands between two standard ratings is resolved by the protection rules, not by ordering a breaker in the calculated size.

The standard ratings (240.6(A)):
• 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100
• 110, 125, 150, 175, 200, 225, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, 600
• 700, 800, 1000, 1200, 1600, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000
Fuses also have additional standard ratings of 1, 3, 6, 10, and 601 amperes. Note the gaps crews trip on: there is no standard 105A, 130A, or 275A device — a calculation landing there resolves to a standard rating under the protection rules.
sections.on_the_job: When a load calculation lands at a nonstandard number, write the next step as a choice between the standard ratings on either side and record which rule you used. Do not write a nonstandard breaker size on a material list. Example: the optional-method calculation for a Marion Oaks house lands at 130 A. There is no standard 130 A breaker — the material list gets the standard size the protection rules point to, and the calc sheet shows the step that was taken.

nec2023_change.change: Ten amps moved into the standard ratings table, so 10-amp breakers are now standard along with fuses. New 240.6(D) covers breakers whose trip setting can be changed remotely. Table 240.6(A) now starts at 10 amps, making 10 a standard size for inverse-time breakers as well as fuses.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.6 Standard breaker and fuse sizes

sections.why_it_exists: Breakers and fuses are built, listed and stocked in the standard steps. If every calculation produced its own device size, panels could not be planned, breakers could not be swapped, and an inspector could not check a rating at a glance. The steps also leave room for the protection rules to work: a load that lands between two steps is resolved by rule, not by inventing a size.

The second trap is putting 10 A in the 2020 standard table: in 2020, 10 A is only an additional standard rating for fuses. It joins the main table in 2023 (see the 2020 vs 2023 box).
