sections.title: Feeder taps — the 10 ft and 25 ft rules
sections.plain_explanation:
A tap is a conductor that leaves a feeder without its own overcurrent protection at the point of supply, protected instead by the feeder's larger device. That is permitted only inside the fences of this section. The two rules used most:
• The 10 ft tap — tap conductors not over 10 ft long, with ampacity not less than the combined calculated loads and not less than the rating of the equipment, or of the overcurrent device, the tap supplies; the conductors do not extend beyond the panelboard, switchboard or device they supply; they are enclosed in a raceway (except at the termination) and protected from physical damage; and, for field installations where the tap leaves the enclosure or vault it is made in, ampacity not less than one-tenth of the feeder OCPD rating
• The 25 ft tap — tap conductors not over 25 ft long, with ampacity not less than one-third the rating of the feeder's overcurrent device, terminating in a single circuit breaker or single set of fuses that limits the load to the tap ampacity, with the conductors protected from physical damage
Longer taps, outside taps, and transformer taps have their own conditions in this section — a tap that fits neither rule above is not made legal by being short-ish.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: tapping a 400A feeder to feed a 100A panelboard nearby. As a 10 ft tap, the conductors need ampacity of at least 100A (the device supplied) — comfortably over one-tenth of 400A. As a 25 ft tap they would need at least one-third of 400A, about 133A — the longer tap demands the bigger wire. Measure the actual run before choosing which rule you are on. Write the tap length on the plan — the inspector will measure it, and the measurement picks the rule.
sections.figure_idea: A 400A feeder with two taps drawn: a short tap tagged 10 ft rule / one-tenth, and a longer tap tagged 25 ft rule / one-third, each ending in its own breaker.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A tap conductor is protected by a breaker far larger than itself — a tap on a 400A feeder can carry several times its own ampacity before the feeder device reacts. The length limits, the raceway and damage rules, and the ampacity ratios keep that exposure short and survivable, so a fault on the tap clears before the tap conductor cooks.
inspection_fails: Tap measured at 13 ft and built to the 10 ft rule.
25 ft tap ending in a panelboard with no single breaker or fuse set limiting the load.
10 ft tap run open across a ceiling — the rule requires a raceway except at the termination.
Tap conductors extended past the panelboard they supply to pick up a second load.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'The tap is 22 ft, so I used the 10 ft rule's one-tenth ratio.' Length picks the rule first. Past 10 ft the tap is on the 25 ft rule: at least one-third of the feeder device — about 133A of ampacity on a 400A feeder — and a single breaker or fuse set where it ends.

sections.title: Where overcurrent devices may be located
sections.plain_explanation:
Circuit breakers and switches containing fuses must be readily accessible, and installed so the center of the grip of the operating handle, in its highest position, is not more than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or working platform. That height limit does not apply in four cases:
• Busways, under 368.17(C)
• Supplementary overcurrent protection, under 240.10
• Overcurrent devices described in 225.40 and 230.92
• Devices next to the utilization equipment they supply, where access may be by portable means
A tool may be used to reach devices inside listed industrial control panels or similar enclosures. The rest of this section bars devices near easily ignitable material and in clothes closets, and, in dwellings, in bathrooms.
sections.on_the_job: Measure handle height to the top breaker in the panel as installed, including a raised floor or platform change on a remodel. And site the panel early: a closet or bathroom location is a relocation, not a waiver request. On a Florida garage-conversion remodel, the existing panel sat in what became the new bathroom and the top breaker grip measured 6 ft 10 in over the new raised floor — two failures on one panel. It moved to the hallway wall, top grip at 6 ft 5 in, before rough-in.
sections.sharma_note: S-09's back-to-back panel still has to satisfy this section and the working-space rules in Article 110 — a good meter position does not excuse a panel in a closet.
sections.figure_idea: A panel on a wall with a tape from the floor to the top breaker handle at 6 ft 7 in, and a closet door and a bathroom door both crossed out as locations.

nec2023_change.change: The no-breakers-in-bathrooms rule now covers every occupancy and adds showering facilities and locker rooms with showers. A tool can now be needed to open more kinds of enclosures. No breakers or fuses in a bathroom, a shower facility, or a locker room that has showers, whether it's a house, gym or factory (240.24(E)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 240.24 Breakers out of all bathrooms

sections.why_it_exists: A breaker is the disconnect a person reaches for when something is already wrong — smoke, a fault, a flooded room. If it sits too high to grip, behind stored clothes, or in a steamy bathroom, it cannot be reached fast and the enclosure corrodes. The height and location rules keep the handle reachable by an average person standing on the floor, in a dry, clear spot.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 6 ft 7 in measured to the top of the panel, or to the breaker handle in its lowest position. The rule measures to the center of the grip of the operating handle in its highest position, above the floor or working platform. Second trap: the 2020 bathroom ban covers dwellings — the every-occupancy version is 2023.
inspection_fails: Panel in a clothes closet. 240.24 bars overcurrent devices in clothes closets.
Top breaker grip at 6 ft 10 in above the floor. The limit is 6 ft 7 in to the center of the grip, in its highest position.
Panel in a dwelling bathroom. Not permitted in dwellings under the 2020 rule.
Panel sited where the only access is through stored material — not readily accessible.

tables.note: NEC 2023 extends the bathroom ban to every occupancy and adds shower facilities and locker rooms with showers — see the 2020 vs 2023 box.

figures.caption: Handle height, and two places the panel never goes.

page_quiz.question: The center of the grip of the top breaker's handle, in its highest position, may be no higher than:
page_quiz.explain_plain: The limit is 6 ft 7 in, measured to the center of the grip with the handle at its highest, above the floor or working platform.

page_quiz.question: Under NEC 2020, a panelboard may be installed in:
choices: A hallway wall with working space
page_quiz.explain_plain: The hallway wall complies; closets, dwelling bathrooms, and spots near easily ignitable material are barred.

choices: The main breaker of a house panel
Every breaker in a commercial panel
page_quiz.explain_plain: Supplementary protection under 240.10 is one of the four exceptions to the height limit.

sections.title: Breaker markings — and the slash-rating trap
sections.plain_explanation: A circuit breaker's markings are working information: ampere rating and voltage rating are marked by the manufacturer, the interrupting rating is marked on breakers with an interrupting rating other than 5,000A (240.83(C)), and special-duty markings tell you where the breaker may be applied — SWD for breakers used to switch fluorescent or HID lighting loads, HACR for heating, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment. Voltage markings come in two forms. A straight-rated breaker (e.g., 240V) may be applied where the nominal voltage between any two conductors does not exceed its rating. A slash-rated breaker (120/240V, 480Y/277V) may be applied only in a solidly grounded circuit where no conductor's nominal voltage to ground exceeds the lower value and the voltage between any two conductors does not exceed the higher value — which is why a slash-rated breaker does not belong on the high leg of a 240V delta system (208V to ground) or on a corner-grounded system.
sections.on_the_job: On a high-leg delta panel, read the breaker voltage marking before you land the high leg: a 120/240 slash-rated breaker is the wrong breaker there even though the amp rating matches. Check the marking on the breaker in your hand, not the one you expected to find in the box. On a small commercial service call in Winter Park, the failed 20A breaker on the high leg gets replaced with a straight 240V Siemens breaker, not the 120/240V slash breaker riding in the truck stock.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: new gear is Siemens. The marking check applies to whatever breaker is actually installed — a substituted breaker with the wrong voltage rating is still the wrong breaker.
sections.figure_idea: Two breaker labels side by side: a '240V' straight rating approved for the high leg, a '120/240V' slash rating crossed out for the high leg, with the SWD and HACR marks called out.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A breaker has to interrupt the arc inside itself when it opens on a fault. If the voltage across the open contacts is higher than the breaker was tested for, the arc can restrike or blow through the case instead of clearing. The slash-rating rule exists because a high leg sits 208V to ground — well over the 120V a 120/240V breaker is built to hold off to ground — even though the load voltage looks like an ordinary 240V.
inspection_fails: Slash-rated 120/240V breaker landed on the high leg of a 240V delta panel.
Breaker switching a fluorescent lighting load with no SWD marking.
Replacement breaker installed with a voltage rating below the system voltage.
Breaker markings painted over or illegible — the rating can no longer be verified.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: a 120/240V breaker 'matches' a 240V high-leg delta because 240 is the bigger number on the label. Wrong — on the high leg the voltage to ground is 208V, which beats the 120V lower number of the slash rating. The lower number is the one that decides where a slash-rated breaker may go.

tables.caption: Straight vs slash voltage ratings
tables.note: A slash rating works only on a solidly grounded system that meets both numbers.

figures.caption: Straight vs slash: on the high leg, the lower number decides.

page_quiz.question: A 120/240V slash-rated breaker may be installed on the high leg of a 240V delta system when…
choices: Never — the high leg is 208V to ground, over the 120V lower rating
The panel is labeled for it
page_quiz.explain_plain: A slash rating caps voltage to ground at the lower number. The high leg sits at 208V to ground.

page_quiz.question: The interrupting rating must be marked on a breaker when it is…
page_quiz.explain_plain: Breakers with an interrupting rating other than 5,000A carry the marking; 5,000A is the assumed floor.

page_quiz.question: A breaker used to switch HID lighting loads must be marked…
page_quiz.explain_plain: SWD is the special-duty marking for switching fluorescent and HID lighting loads.

sections.title: Grounding and bonding — the fault-current path
sections.plain_explanation: Article 250 is the longest and most argued article in this chapter. Grounding connects a system to earth through electrodes; bonding connects metal parts together so a fault has a low-impedance path back to the source that trips the breaker fast. Earth itself is not that fault path — the breaker trips because bonding carries the fault home. Section 250.4 states the performance test the whole article is built to pass: the path must be permanent and continuous, low-impedance, and able to carry the fault current long enough for the overcurrent device to open. When a detail is argued on site, that test settles it. The pages that follow walk the service bond, the electrodes, the sizing tables, and the piping and intersystem bonds in that order.
sections.on_the_job: On every job, trace one imaginary fault with your finger: a hot wire chafes through onto the metal frame of an air handler. The fault current runs on the equipment grounding conductor to the service, crosses the main bonding jumper to the neutral, and rides back out to the source — and the breaker opens on the way. If any link in that loop is missing, painted over, or loose, you have found the defect. On a Sharma 200 A house service the hardware in that loop is sized, not guessed: the main bonding jumper is 4 AWG copper behind 2/0 copper service conductors (250.28), and the grounding electrode conductor comes off Table 250.66 (the 250.50 page).
sections.sharma_note: Torque and termination discipline decide whether this article works in real life. A correctly sized conductor on a loose lug is not a fault path.
sections.figure_idea: A fault-path diagram: a hot conductor touching an appliance frame, fault current traveling the green ground back to the service bond, and the breaker opening.

nec2023_change.change: The hazardous-location bonding rule was reworded for accuracy. Raceways, metal-clad cable, equipment and enclosures still need threaded, threadless or listed bonding fittings, even with a wire-type equipment grounding conductor (EGC). In classified locations, bond with a method from 250.92(B)(2) through (B)(4): wrenchtight threaded entries, tight threadless fittings, or other listed bonding devices.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.100 Bonding in hazardous locations

nec2023_change.change: Plaster rings and extension rings now join metal covers and fittings: each must be fastened to a metal box so the fault path holds, or bonded with a jumper or equipment grounding conductor (EGC). Metal covers, plaster rings, extension rings and metal fittings must be fastened so the fault path holds, or else bonded with a jumper or EGC.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.109 Covers and rings on metal boxes

nec2023_change.change: Cord-and-plug ice makers joined the list of appliances whose exposed metal parts must connect to an equipment grounding conductor (EGC), in homes and other occupancies alike. Ice makers now sit next to refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners in the residential list, 250.114(3).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.114 Ice makers need an EGC

nec2023_change.change: 250.130(C) now covers swapping out a nongrounding snap switch. An equipment grounding conductor (EGC) added for the new switch can land at the same points already allowed for receptacles. Putting a switch with a grounding terminal in an old box with no EGC? Its new EGC can run to any point listed in 250.130(C).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.130 Grounding replaced switches too

nec2023_change.change: A jumper to a metal box now has a size rule: Table 250.122, based on the largest breaker or fuse on circuits in the box. Rules for joining the grounding conductors got clearer too. A bonding jumper to a metal box is now sized from Table 250.122, using the largest breaker or fuse on circuits in that box (250.148(C)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.148 Grounding connections in boxes

nec2023_change.change: The section now says impedance grounded systems, dropping high and neutral, and renames its conductors to match their real jobs. When you can use one hasn't changed. Renamed from high-impedance grounded neutral systems to impedance grounded systems. High and neutral both came out.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.36 Impedance grounded systems

nec2023_change.change: The 2023 edition spells it out: neither ground-fault current nor current on a grounding or bonding connection Article 250 requires counts as objectionable current. Current on a required grounding or bonding connection is not objectionable current (250.6(C)). Don't remove the connection to stop it.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.6 Objectionable current

nec2023_change.change: Mostly a cleanup: 250.70 now splits general rules from the indoor communications strap clamp, and a new note confirms a direct-burial clamp also suits concrete encasement. New note: a clamp listed for direct burial is also suitable for concrete encasement, so it can go on a concrete-encased electrode.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.70 Connections to electrodes

nec2023_change.change: References to the NFPA 780 standard were removed for Informational Note No. 1 and updated for Informational Note No. 2.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 250.106 Lightning Protection Systems

sections.why_it_exists: A breaker only trips when fault current is big, and fault current is only big when the loop back to the source is low-impedance metal the whole way. Dirt is not that loop: a fault dumped into a ground rod may draw only a few amps — nowhere near enough to move a 20 A breaker — while the metal case of a washer sits live at 120 V, waiting for a hand. Bonding builds the metal loop. Grounding ties the system to earth to limit lightning and surge voltage and to hold the voltage to ground steady.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "The ground rods trip the breaker on a fault." They do not. Earth is far too high an impedance to carry fault current back to the source, and 250.4 says plainly that the earth shall not be considered an effective ground-fault current path. The breaker trips because bonding and the equipment grounding conductor carry the fault home on metal.
inspection_fails: Bootleg ground: the neutral jumpered to the ground terminal at a receptacle to fake a grounded outlet on a tester.
Subpanel "grounded" to a local rod with no equipment grounding conductor run back to the service.
Bonding lug landed over paint, or torqued loose, so the fault path is a resistor.
Equipment grounding conductor cut or left unlanded after a device swap into a plastic box.

tables.caption: Three jobs that get mixed up
rows: The system to earth, through electrodes
Limits lightning and surge voltage; holds voltage to ground steady
Makes every enclosure and raceway one continuous fault path
Equipment frames to the service bond
Carries fault current back so the breaker opens

figures.alt: Fault-path loop diagram: a hot conductor touches the frame of an air handler, fault current travels the green equipment grounding conductor back to the service panel, crosses the gold main bonding jumper to the neutral, and returns to the source while the breaker opens; a ground rod below the panel is crossed out with the note that earth is not the fault path.
figures.caption: The loop that trips the breaker is metal the whole way home.

page_quiz.question: What carries fault current back to the source so the breaker trips?
choices: The earth, through the ground rods
The bonded metal path and the equipment grounding conductor
page_quiz.explain_plain: Bonding and the EGC form a low-impedance metal loop; the fault current on that loop is what opens the breaker.

page_quiz.question: Under 250.4, the earth shall not be considered:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.4 states it directly: the earth is not an effective ground-fault current path.

page_quiz.question: Bonding is best defined as:
choices: Connecting a system to a ground rod
Joining metal parts to establish electrical continuity and conductivity
page_quiz.explain_plain: Bonding joins metal parts into one continuous, conductive whole — that continuity is the fault path.

sections.title: What grounding and bonding must accomplish
sections.plain_explanation:
This general section states the performance the rest of Article 250 has to deliver, and it splits the work into two jobs:
• Grounding — connecting the system and equipment to earth. It limits the voltage imposed by lightning, line surges, and accidental contact with higher-voltage lines, and it stabilizes the voltage to ground during normal operation.
• Bonding — connecting metal parts together and back to the source in one continuous, low-impedance path that can carry fault current long enough for the overcurrent device to open.
The section states plainly that the earth is not an effective ground-fault current path and must not be used as the sole equipment grounding conductor. When a specific installation rule is unclear, this section is the test it has to pass.
sections.on_the_job: On a Florida slab house with a meter-main outside and the panel inside, run this page as a checklist before you call the rough-in. The grounding electrode system is bonded together at the service (250.50). The main bonding jumper lands at the meter-main, where the neutral meets ground. An equipment grounding conductor runs with the feeder to the inside panel, and the neutral is not bonded to ground again downstream (250.24(A)(5)). One rod by itself must prove 25 ohms or less, or a second rod goes in (250.53(A)(2)). Then ask the question this section asks: will it trip the breaker, fast, every time? If any link in that chain is missing, the honest answer is no.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A hot conductor that faults to a metal enclosure puts that enclosure at line voltage. If the only way back is through the earth, the path impedance is so high that only a few amperes flow — far too little to trip a breaker — and the enclosure sits energized, waiting for a hand to complete the circuit through a body. A bonded, low-impedance path back to the source lets a heavy fault current flow for the fraction of a second the breaker needs to open. Earth grounding handles lightning and surges; bonding is what clears faults.
inspection_fails: No equipment grounding conductor run with the circuit — the installer relied on the ground rod to clear faults.
Neutral bonded to ground again in a subpanel downstream of the service disconnect (250.24(A)(5)).
Grounding electrode conductor spliced with a split bolt instead of an irreversible compression connector or exothermic weld (250.64(C)).
Metal interior water piping left unbonded (250.104).
sections.exam_trap: The tempting answer says a ground rod at the panel 'gives fault current a path to earth so the breaker trips.' It is wrong twice. The rod's job is lightning and surges, and the earth is far too high in impedance to clear a fault. The breaker trips because of the bonded path back to the source (250.4(A)(5)).

rows: Limits lightning and surge voltage; stabilizes voltage to ground

figures.alt: Comparison panel for a fault to a metal enclosure: the earth-only path through a ground rod is too high in impedance to trip the breaker, while the bonded equipment grounding path back to the source clears the fault.
figures.caption: Fault clearing runs on the bonded path, not on the earth.

page_quiz.question: A hot conductor faults to a metal enclosure. What makes the breaker trip?
choices: The ground rod carries the fault into the earth
The bonded low-impedance path back to the source carries enough current to open it
The surge protector absorbs the fault
page_quiz.explain_plain: Fault clearing needs a low-impedance path back to the source so a heavy fault current flows and the breaker opens. The earth cannot do it.

page_quiz.question: Under 250.4, the earth may be used as:
choices: Part of the grounding electrode system, but never the sole fault path
The neutral return for a subpanel
A substitute for bonding metal piping
page_quiz.explain_plain: The earth is not an effective ground-fault current path and must not be the sole equipment grounding conductor.

page_quiz.question: A single ground rod measures more than 25 ohms to earth. The standard fix is:
choices: Connect it to the water pipe and stop
page_quiz.explain_plain: A single rod must show 25 ohms or less, or it is supplemented with a second electrode.

sections.title: How grounding and bonding connections are made
sections.plain_explanation:
Grounding and bonding connections are made only by the methods 250.8(A) lists:
• Listed pressure connectors
• Terminal bars
• Pressure connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment
• Exothermic welding
• Machine-screw fasteners that engage at least two threads, or are secured with a nut
• Thread-forming machine screws that engage at least two threads in the enclosure
• Connections that are part of a listed assembly
• Other listed means
Connections to an electrode itself follow 250.70 — listed lugs, pressure connectors or clamps, or exothermic welding. Solder alone is never the connection: a soldered-only joint can melt open during a fault, which is the exact moment the path is needed. One screw or terminal takes one conductor, unless the device is listed and identified for more.
sections.on_the_job: Crimp, clamp, or weld it — never solder-only. On a service call, two grounds landed under one ordinary green screw and a soldered splice in the grounding path are both rework items: correct them with listed connectors while the panel is open. On a 200 A service change in Ocala, the old grounding electrode conductor was spliced with solder and tape inside the wall. It was replaced with a listed irreversible crimp before the new meter-main went on — the splice you cannot see is the one that fails.
sections.figure_idea: Connection lineup: listed pressure connector, exothermic weld, and two-thread machine screw marked approved; a solder-only joint crossed out.
sections.why_it_exists: The grounding path has to survive the worst second of the building's life — a fault that drives hundreds or thousands of amperes through it until the breaker opens. A connection that is merely touching, soldered, or hanging on one thread can melt or tear open under that current. The listed methods are the ones tested to carry fault current and stay together.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is solder: a neat soldered splice looks permanent and tests continuous, but solder alone is not a permitted connection method — it can melt open under fault current. Second trap: a machine screw engaging one thread. The rule is at least two threads, or a nut.
inspection_fails: Grounding electrode conductor spliced with solder only. Not a 250.8 method.
Two grounding conductors under one terminal screw that is not listed for two.
Sheet-metal screw used as the bonding fastener — it does not engage two threads like a machine screw.
Ground clamp on the rod not listed for the purpose, loose enough to turn by hand.

tables.caption: Connection check
tables.note: The full method list is 250.8(A). Connections at the electrode itself follow 250.70.

figures.alt: Four connection panels: a listed pressure connector, an exothermic weld, and a machine screw engaging two threads, each marked with a green check; a solder-only joint crossed out in red because solder alone is never a permitted connection.
figures.caption: Three connections that carry a fault, and one that does not.

page_quiz.question: Which connection is permitted for a bonding jumper?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Bonding connections are made by the listed methods in 250.8(A) — a listed pressure connector is one of them.

choices: Engage at least two threads or be secured with a nut
page_quiz.explain_plain: Two threads minimum, or a nut — one thread is not a connection.

sections.title: Which AC systems must be grounded
sections.plain_explanation:
Some AC systems are required to be grounded, and the common Florida systems are on the list:
• A system that can be grounded so the maximum voltage to ground stays at or below 150 volts must be grounded
• Systems whose neutral is used as a circuit conductor are grounded systems — the 120/240V house service, and the 208Y/120V and 480Y/277V commercial services
Grounding the system fixes the voltage to ground, gives lightning and surge energy a reference, and makes the fault-clearing path on the 250.4 page possible. Whether a delta system is grounded, and which conductor is the grounded one (250.26), is set by this article — never by field preference. An ungrounded system is not a shortcut around bonding: the equipment grounding and bonding rules still apply to it.
sections.on_the_job: Identify the system before you bond anything: wye or delta, which conductor (if any) is grounded, and where the single grounding point is. On an unfamiliar commercial service, the transformer configuration answers these questions — get it from the drawings or the utility, not by testing until something looks right. On a 480Y/277V retail service in Winter Park, the drawings showed the neutral grounded at the service only; the separately derived system in the tenant space needed its own grounding arrangement under 250.30, not a second bond on the service neutral.
sections.figure_idea: Three service diagrams — 120/240 single-phase, 208Y/120, 480Y/277 — each with the grounded conductor marked and the single grounding point circled.
sections.why_it_exists: An ungrounded or floating system has no fixed voltage to earth, so the first ground fault raises the other conductors to full line voltage above ground and delivers no fault current to trip anything. Grounding the system pins the voltage to ground, gives lightning and surges a reference point, and lets a ground fault draw enough current to open the breaker.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is '480Y/277 cannot be a grounded system because 277 volts to ground is over the 150-volt limit.' The 150-volt test is only one path onto the list. A wye system whose neutral is used as a circuit conductor is grounded regardless of its voltage to ground.
inspection_fails: Neutral bonded at the service and again at a subpanel. One grounding point for the system; downstream neutrals stay isolated.
Corner-grounded delta treated as if it were ungrounded — the grounded phase never identified or marked.
Grounding electrode conductor landed before anyone confirmed which conductor the system grounds. Identify the system first.
480Y/277V service roughed in as if it were ungrounded — the neutral never connected to the grounding electrode system.

sections.title: Grounding at the service — and nowhere downstream
sections.plain_explanation:
At the service, three connections come together in the service equipment:
• The grounding electrode conductor lands on the grounded conductor (the neutral).
• The main bonding jumper ties the neutral to the equipment grounding conductors and to the enclosure.
• From that one point on, the neutral carries load current and the grounding system carries fault current.
That is the one place in a premises system where neutral and ground meet. Downstream of the service — in subpanels and feeders — the grounded conductor is kept isolated from equipment grounds and enclosures, so normal neutral current never travels on metal parts and fault current has one clear path home.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma's standard is the S-09 back-to-back: the outdoor Siemens meter-main is the service equipment, so the main bonding jumper and the grounding electrode conductor land there. On a 200 A service with 2/0 copper service conductors, the main bonding jumper is 4 AWG copper, sized from Table 250.102(C)(1) by way of 250.28. The indoor panel is a subpanel: four-wire feeder, neutral bar isolated and floating, ground bar bonded to the can, bonding screw left out. Photograph the first subpanel on a job and check it against this page.
sections.sharma_note: S-09's back-to-back service is where Sharma's bond is made; every panel downstream of it is wired isolated-neutral, no exceptions for a detached building panel that is actually a subpanel — see 250.32 for the separate-building case.

sections.why_it_exists: Add a second bond in a subpanel and neutral current splits: part of it rides the conduit, the water pipe and every equipment ground back to the service. Metal that should sit at zero volts now carries current every minute of the day, and if that neutral ever loosens, full load current can push onto parts a person can touch. One bond at the service keeps normal current on the neutral, where it belongs, and reserves the grounding path for faults — so a fault draws the heavy current that trips the breaker fast.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "Bond the neutral in every panel — more grounds are safer." Wrong. Every bond past the service puts load current on metal parts, all day long. The only neutral-to-ground connection in the premises system is the main bonding jumper at the service. (A separately derived system, and a separate building under 250.32, follow their own pages and their own rules.)

sections.title: Main and system bonding jumpers
sections.plain_explanation:
The bonding jumper is the conductor or connection that ties the grounded conductor, the equipment grounding system, and the enclosure together at the service, and the system bonding jumper does the same job for a separately derived system. This section covers their material and how they are sized — for the main bonding jumper, by reference to the same sizing table used for the grounding electrode conductor, with the limits the section states. A jumper that is present but undersized or poorly landed does not do the job.

The sizing numbers: a main bonding jumper is sized from Table 250.102(C)(1) by the size of the largest ungrounded service conductor (250.28(D)(1)). Where the service conductors are larger than 1100 kcmil copper (1750 kcmil aluminum), the table stops and the jumper must be not less than 12-1/2 percent of the cross-sectional area of the largest phase conductor. On ordinary house services the table rows are the whole answer: 8 AWG copper behind a 100A service on 4 AWG copper conductors, 4 AWG copper behind a 200A service on 2/0 copper.
sections.on_the_job: Factory-installed straps and screws count only when they are the listed means for that equipment and actually installed. On a service change, verify the jumper exists before you call for inspection — it is a small part with a whole article riding on it. On a 200 A Siemens meter-main with 2/0 copper service conductors, the table answer is a 4 AWG copper jumper — confirm the factory strap is the listed means for that can and that it is actually landed, not still in the parts bag.

sections.why_it_exists: The main bonding jumper is the link that ties the enclosure, the equipment grounding system and the grounded conductor together at one point — the service. When a hot conductor faults to the enclosure, that jumper is part of the path that carries the fault back to the source so the overcurrent device opens. A jumper that is missing or undersized is a bottleneck in that path: the enclosure can sit energized while the breaker never trips.

Bonding jumper present but landed loose, so the connection is not doing the job.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the main bonding jumper from the service breaker rating — or, on a service over 1100 kcmil copper, grabs the largest row in the table. The table is keyed to the largest ungrounded service conductor, not the breaker. And past 1100 kcmil copper (1750 kcmil aluminum) the table stops: the jumper must be not less than 12-1/2 percent of the largest phase conductor's cross-sectional area.

sections.title: Separately derived systems — generators and transformers
sections.plain_explanation:
A separately derived system (SDS) is a source — a transformer, or a generator whose neutral is switched — that has no direct electrical connection to the supply system's circuit conductors; the two systems touch only through grounding and bonding. Because it is its own system, it needs its own grounding arrangement:
• A system bonding jumper connecting the derived neutral to the equipment grounds and enclosure, made at the source or at the first disconnecting means — at one point only; both locations are permitted only where doing so does not create a parallel path for neutral current (250.30(A)(1) Exception No. 2)
• A grounding electrode conductor run to the building or structure grounding electrode system, as near as practicable to the point where the system bonding jumper connects (250.30(A)(4)), sized from the derived conductors by the same table used at a service (250.66)
A new rod is only needed where the building has no electrode system. A ground rod driven beside a generator, without the bonding jumper and electrode conductor, is decoration, not grounding.
sections.on_the_job: The transfer switch decides the design. If the switch does not switch the neutral, the generator is usually NOT separately derived, and the neutral stays bonded only at the service. If it does switch the neutral, the generator is an SDS and gets its bonding jumper at the generator end. Confirm which design the job has before anyone bonds a generator neutral — two bonding points put neutral current on the grounding path.

sections.why_it_exists: A derived system has no metallic path back to the utility source, so a ground fault inside it has no way to trip anything until the system gets its own bond and electrode connection. That bond is also a hazard when doubled: two neutral-to-ground bonds split neutral current onto equipment grounds and enclosures, where it heats connections and shocks anyone who touches metal.

GEC for the derived system sized by guess instead of Table 250.66 from the derived conductors.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is “every generator is separately derived.” A generator fed through a transfer switch that does not switch the neutral is usually NOT separately derived, and bonding its neutral creates the second bond the rule forbids. The switch gear decides, not the generator.

sections.title: A separate building fed by a feeder
sections.plain_explanation:
When a feeder or branch circuit supplies a second building or structure, that building is treated almost like a service — but it is not one. The building needs:
• A disconnecting means for the supply (225.31)
• Its own grounding electrode system (250.32(A)). Exception: a building fed by a single branch circuit, individual or multiwire, that includes an equipment grounding conductor needs no electrode system
• An equipment grounding conductor run with the feeder (250.32(B)(1)), sized from 250.122. The disconnect and the electrodes connect to that EGC
• The grounded conductor (neutral) is NOT bonded at the separate building. A neutral run with the feeder stays isolated from the EGC and the electrodes — the one neutral-to-ground bond stays at the service
One narrow exception, for existing installations only: the grounded conductor may be connected at the separate building if all three are true — no EGC was run with the supply, there are no continuous metallic paths bonded to the grounding system in both buildings (a metal water line between them kills it), and ground-fault protection of equipment is not installed on the supply side. That grounded conductor cannot be smaller than the larger of 220.61 and 250.122. The Article 250 companion to the Article 225 pages.
sections.on_the_job: Detached garage behind an Ocala house, fed from the house panel: run a four-wire feeder — two hots, an isolated neutral, and an EGC. At the garage, set the disconnect, land the EGC on the ground bar, and drive two 8 ft rods 6 ft apart, bonded to that bar; a single rod is enough only with a 25-ohm test on file. Leave the panel's bonding screw out. If you open an older garage panel and find a three-wire feed with the neutral bonded, do not just copy it: check the three exception conditions first, and write down what you found.
sections.why_it_exists: Bond the neutral a second time and normal neutral current splits onto every parallel metal path — the EGC, the water piping, the earth itself. That objectionable current raises touch voltage on equipment, corrodes buried metal, and can leave bonded parts live if the neutral ever opens. One bond at the service, plus a separate EGC, gives fault current a solid metal path home so the breaker trips instead of the equipment case going hot.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'A separate building gets its own service, so bond the neutral there like a main.' Wrong — a feeder is not a service. The bond stays at the service; the separate building gets electrodes and an EGC, with the neutral isolated. The only re-bond allowed is the existing-installation exception, and it dies the moment an EGC is run or a metal water line links the buildings.
inspection_fails: Neutral bonded in the detached garage panel — bonding screw in or strap landed — putting neutral current on the EGC and the water piping.
No grounding electrode system at the separate building fed by a feeder.
New feeder run as three wires with no EGC, claiming the existing-installation exception on new work.
Ground rods driven at the garage but never bonded to the panel ground bar.

sections.title: Portable generators — frame grounding and the neutral bond
sections.plain_explanation: A portable generator is not automatically a separately derived system. Where the generator supplies only equipment mounted on it and cord-and-plug equipment plugged into its own receptacles, the generator frame itself serves as the grounding reference and the Code does not require a ground rod to be driven for it; the frame is bonded to the equipment grounding terminals of its receptacles. Whether the neutral is bonded to the frame depends on the generator's design — bonded-neutral and floating-neutral portables both exist, and they behave differently with GFCI receptacles and transfer equipment. The picture changes when the generator feeds premises wiring: then the transfer equipment and the rules on the 250.30 page decide whether the neutral is switched, where the single bonding point is, and what electrode connection is required.
sections.on_the_job: Read the generator's label before connecting it to a house: 'neutral bonded to frame' versus a floating neutral changes the transfer-switch design. The field failure is a bonded-neutral portable plugged into a system that also bonds at the service — neutral current on the grounding path and nuisance GFCI trips. That is why Sharma's hurricane-season answer is always the same: a listed inlet and an interlock or transfer switch, with the generator's neutral arrangement checked against the transfer design before the first storm, not during it.
sections.figure_idea: Portable generator with its receptacle panel: frame bond shown, neutral-bond label called out, and a crossed-out back-feed cord beside it.
sections.florida_note: Hurricane season makes portable generators a standing Florida case — and homeowners back-feeding a panel through a dryer receptacle is a lethal, illegal arrangement. Sharma's answer is a listed inlet with an interlock or transfer switch, sized and bonded per the design, every time.

sections.why_it_exists: A generator connected the wrong way can kill somebody who never touched it. Back-feeding a panel energizes the service and the utility lines outside, where a line worker expects a dead circuit. A second neutral bond puts neutral current on grounding paths and metal frames. The frame bond and the single neutral bond are what decide where fault current and neutral current actually go.

Feeding only cord-and-plug loads from its own receptacles, the frame is the grounding reference and no rod is required. The electrode question starts only when the generator feeds premises wiring, and then 250.30 and the transfer equipment decide it.

sections.title: The grounding electrode system — all of it, bonded together
sections.plain_explanation:
Every grounding electrode that is present at a building must be bonded together into one grounding electrode system. You cannot pick the easiest electrode and ignore the others. The electrodes 250.52(A) recognizes:
• Metal underground water pipe with at least 10 ft in direct contact with the earth (it must be supplemented by another electrode)
• Metal in-ground support structure in direct contact with the earth
• Concrete-encased electrode: at least 20 ft of ½ in or larger rebar, or bare 4 AWG or larger copper, in at least 2 in of concrete in a footing or foundation in contact with the earth
• Ground ring: at least 20 ft of bare 2 AWG or larger copper, at least 30 in deep
• Rod and pipe electrodes: at least 8 ft in contact with soil; rods at least 5/8 in diameter unless listed
• Plate electrodes: at least 2 sq ft exposed to soil
• Other local metal underground systems or structures
Where none of these is present, you install a rod, pipe, plate or ring. In an existing building, a concrete-encased electrode is not required if reaching it would disturb the concrete (250.50 Exception).
sections.on_the_job: New slab home: the footing rebar is the best electrode on the job, and the chance to use it ends when the concrete is poured. Before the pour, confirm the qualifying rebar in the footing and a stub-up or bare 4 AWG copper tail near the meter-main. Florida water services are usually PVC or PEX, so the water line is not an electrode, but interior metal water piping still gets bonded under 250.104. If rods are also driven, they are present electrodes and must be bonded in. A single rod needs a second rod unless a 25-ohm test is on file. Land the GEC at the meter-main, where the main bonding jumper is.

sections.why_it_exists: One electrode can corrode, dry out or be cut by a backhoe. Bonding every electrode present gives one connection to earth that limits voltage from lightning, utility surges and accidental contact with higher-voltage lines, and keeps buried metal at the same potential. It does not clear faults: the earth is not an effective fault path (250.4(A)(5)). The equipment grounding conductor back to the source clears faults.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 20 ft of ½ in rebar or bare 4 AWG copper, encased in at least 2 in of concrete.

page_quiz.question: Largest GEC ever required when it is the only connection to ground rods?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.66(A) caps the rod portion at 6 AWG copper regardless of service size.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 2/0 or 3/0 copper reads 4 AWG copper, and a water pipe electrode has no cap.

sections.title: Electrodes that are permitted — and the ones that are not
sections.plain_explanation:
This section lists what may serve as a grounding electrode, from underground water pipe with its conditions, through building steel and concrete-encased electrodes — at least 20 ft of the stated rebar or bare copper conductor encased in the foundation — to rods, pipes, and plates. It also lists what may not be used, which includes metal underground gas piping and aluminum electrodes. A water pipe electrode has its own supplementing rule, covered with the installation section.

The electrode specifications in numbers:
• Metal underground water pipe — at least 10 ft of pipe in direct contact with the earth
• Concrete-encased electrode — at least 20 ft of 1/2 in or larger rebar, or at least 20 ft of bare 4 AWG copper conductor, encased in at least 2 in of concrete in the footing or foundation
• Ground ring — at least 20 ft of bare 2 AWG copper, buried at least 30 in below grade
• Rod and pipe electrodes — at least 8 ft long in contact with the soil; pipe not smaller than 3/4 in trade size; rods not smaller than 5/8 in diameter unless listed for the use
• Plate electrodes — at least 2 sq ft of surface exposed to the surrounding soil
sections.on_the_job: The concrete-encased electrode is the one to coordinate with the builder: 20 ft of qualifying rebar or conductor, encased as the section requires, with an accessible connection. Confirm it with the concrete crew before the pour, in writing on the job notes. On a Florida slab home the crew's default set is the concrete-encased electrode in the footing plus the rods the AHJ expects; Florida water services are usually PVC or PEX, so do not count a water pipe that is not metal in the earth for 10 ft.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The electrode is the building's one connection to earth for lightning, utility surges and line-to-ground faults on the supply side. Each permitted type has a proven minimum size and contact with the soil; below that minimum the connection is too weak or corrodes away too fast to trust. The banned list is just as important: a gas pipe must never carry electrical fault energy, and aluminum corrodes in soil and concrete.
inspection_fails: Concrete-encased electrode short of 20 ft, or the stub-up cut off before the GEC lands.
Metal gas piping bonded in as a grounding electrode — prohibited by 250.52(B).
Ground rod driven less than 8 ft, or a rod under 5/8 in that is not listed.
Water pipe electrode with no supplemental electrode (250.53(D)).
Aluminum electrode, or an aluminum GEC in direct contact with concrete or earth.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps: counting a metal underground gas pipe as an electrode — it is prohibited, not just discouraged — and accepting 10 ft of rebar as a concrete-encased electrode. The Ufer needs 20 ft; 10 ft is the water pipe number.

page_quiz.explain_plain: At least 20 ft of ½ in or larger rebar, or 20 ft of bare 4 AWG copper, in at least 2 in of concrete.

page_quiz.question: Which of these may NOT be used as a grounding electrode?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.52(B) prohibits metal underground gas piping — and aluminum electrodes.

page_quiz.question: A ground ring must be buried at least:
page_quiz.explain_plain: At least 20 ft of bare 2 AWG copper buried at least 30 in below grade.

sections.title: Installing electrodes — rods, depth, and the second rod
sections.plain_explanation:
Electrodes must be installed as this section requires: driven or buried to the depths it states, kept as close as practicable to each other and to the service, and supplemented where a single rod, pipe, or plate does not meet the stated resistance to earth — 25 ohms or less — or is not tested at all. In practice that means a second rod, spaced at least 6 ft from the first, on almost every job. Rod connections must be accessible or of the irreversible or exothermic type the article allows where they are buried.

The installation numbers:
• Rod, pipe, and plate electrodes — at least 8 ft of the electrode in contact with the soil, with the top end flush with or below grade level unless the connection is protected
• Two rods — spaced at least 6 ft apart; the 6 ft is a floor, and wider spacing makes the pair work better
• A single rod, pipe, or plate may stand alone only with a measured resistance to earth of 25 ohms or less — without that measurement on file, the second electrode is required, not optional
sections.on_the_job: Drive two rods at least 6 ft apart unless you have a tested 25-ohm-or-less result in the job file. Keep the grounding electrode conductor run short, straight, and protected where it is exposed. On a 200A slab house in Marion Oaks, plan on two 8 ft rods from the start: drive the first, clamp the grounding electrode conductor, then drive the second at least 6 ft away and land the same run on it — no test instrument, no argument at inspection.
sections.figure_idea: Two ground rods driven flush, spaced with a 6 ft tape between them, and the conductor clamped to each in turn on its way to the service.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The electrode system gives lightning and surge energy a path into the earth and holds the service near earth potential. A single rod in dry sand can measure far above 25 ohms — the connection to earth is then mostly wishful thinking. Two rods, spread apart so their resistance areas do not overlap, bring the pair down where one rod alone could not.
inspection_fails: Single ground rod with no 25-ohm test result in the job file.
Two rods driven 3 ft apart — under the 6 ft minimum spacing.
Rod left sticking above grade with the clamp connection unprotected.
Buried rod connection made with a clamp not listed for the purpose — not accessible, irreversible, or exothermic.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'one 8 ft rod is always enough — the second rod is just belt and suspenders.' Wrong. A single rod, pipe, or plate stands alone only with a measured resistance to earth of 25 ohms or less. No measurement on file means the supplemental electrode is required.

tables.note: Wider rod spacing works better — 6 ft is the floor, not the target.

page_quiz.question: A single ground rod may stand alone only when…
choices: Its measured resistance to earth is 25 ohms or less
page_quiz.explain_plain: Without a measured 25 Ω or less on file, a supplemental electrode is required.

page_quiz.question: Two rod electrodes must be spaced at least…
page_quiz.explain_plain: 6 ft is the minimum spacing — and wider works better.

page_quiz.question: How much of a rod electrode must be in contact with the soil?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Rod, pipe, and plate electrodes need at least 8 ft in contact with the soil, top flush with or below grade unless protected.

sections.title: Installing the grounding electrode conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
The grounding electrode conductor is sized on the 250.66 page; this section is how it must be run:
• Continuous, in one unbroken length, without a splice or joint — except splices made with irreversible compression connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment, or by exothermic welding
• Bare or covered aluminum or copper-clad aluminum GECs without an extruded polymeric covering may not be installed where subject to corrosive conditions or in direct contact with concrete; terminations inside listed enclosures identified for the environment are allowed within 18 in. of the enclosure bottom; outside buildings or enclosures, they may not be terminated within 18 in. of the earth
• Where exposed, a conductor 6 AWG or larger may follow the surface of the building construction without a raceway where it is securely fastened and not subject to physical damage; smaller conductors, and any run exposed to damage, must be protected — in rigid metal conduit, IMC, EMT, schedule 80 PVC, RTRC-XW, or cable armor, or another method this section lists
• A ferrous metal raceway or armor enclosing the conductor must be electrically continuous and bonded to the conductor at both ends — an unbonded steel sleeve chokes the fault path it was meant to protect
sections.on_the_job: Plan the run as one piece from the service to the electrode before anything is cut. A grounding electrode conductor that comes up short gets replaced or extended by an irreversible splice — never by a split bolt that will end up buried in a wall or a trench.
sections.figure_idea: A grounding electrode conductor run from panel to rod in one unbroken line, with a callout at a steel sleeve showing bonds at both ends.

nec2023_change.change: New 250.64(G): a grounding electrode conductor (GEC) can't pass through an enclosure's ventilation openings. Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening. A GEC can't pass through a ventilation opening in an enclosure (250.64(G)). Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.64 No GECs through vent openings

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.64: New 250.64(G): a grounding electrode conductor (GEC) can't pass through an enclosure's ventilation openings. Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening. A GEC can't pass through a ventilation opening in an enclosure (250.64(G)). Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The GEC is the path that ties the electrode system to the service. A splice that corrodes, a split bolt that loosens, or a steel sleeve that chokes the conductor all break that path silently — nothing trips and nothing looks wrong until lightning or a fault finds the weak point. One unbroken, protected, properly bonded run is what keeps the connection real for the life of the building.
inspection_fails: GEC spliced with a split bolt inside a wall or trench.
Steel sleeve or ferrous raceway around the GEC with no bonds at the ends.
8 AWG GEC run exposed on the building surface with no raceway or armor (250.64(B)).
Bare aluminum GEC terminated within 18 in of the earth outside the building.
GEC cut short and extended with a mechanical connector instead of an irreversible splice.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answers name the split bolt as an acceptable GEC splice. It is not: splices must be irreversible compression connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment, or exothermic welds. The second trap is forgetting that a ferrous raceway around the GEC must be bonded at both ends.

A wire connector rated for the size
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.64(C): irreversible compression connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment, or exothermic welding — nothing else.

page_quiz.question: An exposed 6 AWG copper GEC may run on the building surface without a raceway when:
choices: It is securely fastened and not subject to physical damage
page_quiz.explain_plain: 6 AWG or larger may follow the surface if securely fastened and not subject to damage; smaller conductors need protection.

page_quiz.question: A ferrous metal raceway enclosing a GEC must be:

page_quiz.explain_plain: It must be electrically continuous and bonded at both ends, or it chokes the fault path.

sections.title: Sizing the grounding electrode conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
The grounding electrode conductor is sized from Table 250.66 by the size of the largest service-entrance conductor, not by the amperage of the service disconnect alone. Read the table across: the largest service conductor picks the row, and the row gives the GEC — copper or aluminum.
The section then caps what is actually required for particular electrodes:
• The portion of the GEC that is the sole connection to a rod, pipe, or plate electrode never has to be larger than 6 AWG copper (250.66(A))
• The portion that is the sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode never has to be larger than 4 AWG copper (250.66(B))
• The portion that is the sole connection to a ground ring never has to be larger than the ring conductor itself (250.66(C))
The table size governs a run that serves the whole electrode system; the caps limit a run to one kind of electrode. Aluminum and copper-clad conductors used for this purpose have material and installation limits in the surrounding sections (see 250.64).
sections.on_the_job:
Read the service conductor size off the actual conductors, then open the table — a 200A service on compact conductors is not automatically the row you expect. Where one conductor serves several electrodes, size and cap it electrode by electrode as the section directs.

The two house rows, worked: a 100A service on 4 AWG copper or 2 AWG aluminum service conductors reads the first row — 8 AWG copper grounding electrode conductor. A 200A service on 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum reads the third row — 4 AWG copper. Those two answers cover most Sharma services before the per-electrode caps are applied.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The GEC carries lightning and surge energy and holds the service at earth potential, so it is sized from the service conductors — in proportion to the energy the service can deliver. The caps recognize the other end of the run: a single rod or a concrete-encased electrode cannot usefully take more than a 6 or 4 AWG conductor can carry, so the Code stops requiring copper the electrode cannot use.
inspection_fails: GEC picked from the disconnect size instead of the largest service-entrance conductor.
200 A service on 2/0 copper roughed with an 8 AWG GEC — Table 250.66 reads 4 AWG copper.
6 AWG cap applied to the run to a metal water pipe electrode — the cap is only for rod, pipe, and plate electrodes.
Concrete-encased run installed at 6 AWG where the table reads above the cap — the required size is the 4 AWG cap of 250.66(B).
sections.exam_trap: Running the full Table 250.66 size out to a pair of ground rods on a 400 A service and calling the extra copper safer. The rod portion never has to exceed 6 AWG copper (250.66(A)). The dangerous mirror image: capping the run to a metal underground water pipe at 6 AWG. The (A) cap covers rod, pipe, and plate electrodes — a water pipe electrode takes the full table size.

tables.caption: Table 250.66: grounding electrode conductor (NEC 2020)
tables.note: Caps: sole connection to rod, pipe or plate electrodes, 6 AWG Cu max (250.66(A)); to a concrete-encased electrode, 4 AWG Cu max (250.66(B)); to a ground ring, not larger than the ring conductor (250.66(C)). A metal water pipe electrode takes the full table size — it is not the “pipe” of 250.66(A).

figures.alt: Flowchart for sizing the grounding electrode conductor: start from the largest service-entrance conductor, read Table 250.66, then apply the cap for the electrode — 6 AWG copper for rods, 4 AWG for a concrete-encased electrode, ring size for a ground ring.
figures.caption: Table first, then the cap for the electrode it lands on.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 2/0 or 3/0 copper reads across to a 4 AWG copper GEC.

page_quiz.question: Largest GEC ever required when it is the only connection to ground rods?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.66(A) caps the rod portion at 6 AWG copper regardless of service size.

page_quiz.question: Largest GEC required as the sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.66(B) caps the concrete-encased portion at 4 AWG copper.

sections.title: Connections to electrodes — accessibility and continuity
sections.plain_explanation:
Grounding electrode conductor connections must be made so they stay effective: clamps and connectors listed for the electrode and the conductor, connections to a water pipe made at an accessible point within the stated distance of where the pipe enters the building, and the conductor kept continuous or spliced only by the methods this section allows. Interior metal water piping farther into the building is a bonding question, not a substitute electrode connection point.

The stated distance, in numbers: interior metal water piping may be used to interconnect electrodes only within 5 ft of the point where the water pipe enters the building. Beyond that first 5 ft the piping is bonded under 250.104, but it is not part of the electrode path.
sections.on_the_job: Land the water-pipe clamp where it can be inspected, on clean metal, and do not bury a mechanical splice in the grounding electrode conductor run. If a run is cut short on a remodel, replace it or use an allowed irreversible splice — not a split bolt in a wall. On a slab home where the water service enters at the far end of the house from the panel, do not just clamp where the panel is and call the piping run the electrode path: land the connection within the first 5 ft of the entry, or run the grounding electrode conductor to where the pipe enters.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A grounding connection fails silently. A clamp that corrodes, loosens, or gets buried where nobody can inspect it leaves the electrode looking connected while the path is open — and nobody finds out until lightning or a fault needs that path. The accessibility and continuity rules keep the connection inspectable and the conductor unbroken from the service to the electrode.
inspection_fails: GEC clamped to the water pipe well past the first 5 ft from where the pipe enters — the piping run is not the electrode path.
Split-bolt splice in the grounding electrode conductor buried inside a wall.
Clamp landed on painted or corroded pipe with no clean metal contact.
Electrode connection buried below grade with a mechanical clamp where it cannot be inspected.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating any point on the interior metal water piping as an electrode connection because the whole run is metal. Past the first 5 ft from the entry point, that piping is a bonding path under 250.104 — it is not part of the electrode system, and the electrode connection cannot be made there.

page_quiz.question: Interior metal water piping may be used to interconnect electrodes only within how far of the point where the pipe enters the building?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The first 5 ft. Beyond that the piping is bonded under 250.104 but is not part of the electrode path.

An irreversible compression connector or exothermic weld
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.64(C) allows only irreversible compression connectors or exothermic welds as GEC splices.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Clamps and connectors must be listed for the electrode and the conductor, landed on clean metal at an accessible point.

sections.title: The intersystem bonding termination
sections.plain_explanation:
Other systems — telephone, cable, antenna, and similar communications systems — need a place to bond to the electrical grounding system, and this section requires an intersystem bonding termination (IBT) for them, at the service or metering equipment, accessible for connection, with room for the stated number of terminations. It is the small bar or bridge by the meter that keeps a cable installer from clamping onto a random pipe. It does not replace the bonding those systems' own articles require; it gives them the listed place to land.
Where it goes:
• At the service equipment or the metering equipment enclosure, external to the enclosure.
• Also at the disconnecting means of any other building or structure on the property supplied by a feeder or branch circuit.
What it must be (250.94(A)):
• Accessible for connection and inspection.
• A set of terminals with the capacity for connection of not less than three intersystem bonding conductors.
• Mounted so it does not interfere with opening the enclosure.
• Securely mounted and electrically connected to the service equipment, the meter enclosure, or the grounding electrode conductor.
• Listed as grounding and bonding equipment.
sections.on_the_job: Install it where the other utilities actually arrive at the house, and leave it accessible after siding and landscaping. Point it out on the final walk — half its failures are being buried behind finishes. On a Sharma new home, the phone and cable drops land at the meter-main, so the IBT goes on the wall beside it with its terminals free. If the cable installer arrives before the IBT is up, he will clamp the nearest pipe — and the correction lands on us.
sections.figure_idea: A meter base with a small bonding bridge mounted beside it, with telephone and cable ground wires landed on its terminals.

nec2023_change.change: Made minor wording changes in 250.94(A)(4) a and b, and removed Informational Note 1, which did not have much value within the code and did not comply with the NEC Style Manual.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 250.94(A) The lntersystem Bonding Termination Device

sections.why_it_exists: Lightning and utility surges do not respect trade boundaries. If the cable system and the power system sit at different potentials during a surge, the difference equalizes the violent way — arcing between systems, cooking electronics, and shocking whoever touches both at once. One bonded termination point keeps every system at the same potential.
sections.exam_trap: Two wrong answers show up. First: 'the IBT is a grounding electrode' — it is not; it is a termination point that connects other systems to the grounding electrode system. Second: 'landing on the IBT replaces the bonding required by the communications articles' — it does not; those articles still require the bond. The IBT is simply the listed place it lands.
inspection_fails: No IBT at the service — the cable bond is clamped to a hose bibb or a random pipe.
IBT buried behind siding, stucco or landscaping, no longer accessible.
Feeder-supplied detached garage with its own cable drop, but no IBT at its disconnecting means.
IBT mounted where it blocks the meter enclosure door from opening.

tables.caption: The IBT checklist (250.94(A))

figures.caption: The IBT beside the meter-main: one listed landing place for every other system.

page_quiz.question: An intersystem bonding termination must be provided at:

page_quiz.explain_plain: The IBT belongs at the service equipment or metering equipment enclosure — and at the disconnecting means of feeder-supplied buildings.

page_quiz.question: The IBT's set of terminals must have capacity for:
choices: Not less than three intersystem bonding conductors
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.94(A) requires a set of terminals with capacity for not less than three intersystem bonding conductors.

sections.title: Bonding metal piping systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Metal water piping in a building supplied by a grounded system must be bonded, sized and connected as this section directs, and other metal piping that is likely to become energized — gas piping is the standard example — must be bonded as well. The bonding jumper is sized by the circuit or service that could energize the piping, using the tables this section points to. Bonding a pipe is a different job from using it as an electrode, and a pipe can need both treatments in different places.

Which table sizes which bond:
• Metal water piping at a service — the bonding jumper is sized from Table 250.102(C)(1), by the size of the service-entrance conductors (250.104(A)(1)), the same table that sizes the grounding electrode conductor
• Metal water piping in a building supplied by a feeder — sized per 250.102(D), which uses Table 250.122 based on the rating of the feeder overcurrent device (250.104(A)(3))
• Other metal piping, such as gas — the jumper is sized from Table 250.122, by the rating of the circuit that is likely to energize the piping
sections.on_the_job: Trace the water piping bond from the panel to clean pipe, and check any jumper over a water meter or filter so the path stays continuous when the meter is removed. For gas piping, bond per this section and the appliance and piping instructions — and see the Florida note on CSST.
sections.florida_note: CSST gas piping carries manufacturer bonding instructions and FBC Fuel Gas requirements beyond this section. The v1 item L-059 is simplified to this section's rule; do not treat this page as covering CSST bonding.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Any metal pipe that can become energized becomes a building-wide shock path — every faucet, valve and appliance handle is connected to it. A fault, a failed neutral or a lightning event can put voltage on piping that runs to every room. Bonding ties the piping into the grounding system, so that voltage is held down and a fault gets the low-impedance path it needs to open the overcurrent device.
inspection_fails: Metal water piping not bonded at the service.
No bonding jumper across the water meter or filter, so the bond opens when the meter is pulled.
Gas piping with no bonding jumper sized for the circuit that could energize it.
Bond clamp landed on painted or corroded pipe with no clean metal contact.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats bonding the water pipe and using the water pipe as a grounding electrode as one job — or sizes the gas-piping bond out of the service table. They are different jobs with different tables: water piping at a service bonds per Table 250.102(C)(1), while other piping, like gas, bonds per Table 250.122 by the rating of the circuit likely to energize it.

tables.caption: Which table sizes which bond (250.104)

sections.title: Equipment grounding conductors — what counts as one
sections.plain_explanation:
The fault path back to the source may be a wire, or it may be one of the wiring methods this section recognizes as an equipment grounding conductor:
• A wire-type conductor — copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum, bare, covered, or insulated, run with the circuit conductors
• Rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, and electrical metallic tubing — the raceway itself is the ground path, which is why its fittings must be listed and made up tight
• The armor of Type AC cable, with its internal bonding strip; and Type MC cable where the armor, alone or combined with its contained grounding conductor, is listed as the ground path
• Flexible metal conduit and liquidtight flexible metal conduit — only within this section's limits on length (6 ft combined in the ground-return path), fitting listing, and overcurrent rating; outside those limits a wire-type ground must be pulled with the circuit
A method not on this section's list is not a ground path, however solid it looks.
sections.on_the_job: An EMT run with tight listed fittings is its own ground; a loose set-screw coupling is a break in that ground. On a long flexible whip to a motor or rooftop unit, pull the green wire instead of asking the flex to be the path. Count the flex in the ground path, not just the piece in your hand: two 4 ft whips joined in one run put 8 ft of flex in the return path — over the 6 ft combined limit — so a wire-type EGC goes in with the circuit conductors.
sections.figure_idea: Four ground paths drawn side by side: a green wire in conduit, an EMT run with tight fittings, AC armor with its bonding strip, and a flex whip with a wire-type ground pulled inside.

nec2023_change.change: Stainless steel flexible metal conduit (FMC), and liquidtight flex (LFMC) with a stainless core, can't serve as the equipment grounding conductor (EGC) anymore. Add a wire-type EGC or a bonding jumper. Stainless steel FMC doesn't count as the EGC. Install a wire-type EGC, or a bonding jumper that meets 250.102(E)(2) (250.118(A)(5)(f)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.118 Stainless flex as an EGC

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.118: Stainless steel flexible metal conduit (FMC), and liquidtight flex (LFMC) with a stainless core, can't serve as the equipment grounding conductor (EGC) anymore. Add a wire-type EGC or a bonding jumper. Stainless steel FMC doesn't count as the EGC. Install a wire-type EGC, or a bonding jumper that meets 250.102(E)(2) (250.118(A)(5)(f)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The equipment grounding conductor is the path that carries fault current back to the source so the breaker trips in a fraction of a second. That path has to be permanent and low-impedance. A raceway only works as the path while every fitting stays listed and tight — one loose coupling or corroded joint raises the impedance, the fault current drops, the breaker never trips, and the metal case of the equipment sits energized waiting for a hand.
inspection_fails: Loose set-screw EMT coupling left in the ground path — the raceway ground is broken at the joint.
Flexible whip over 6 ft in the ground-return path with no wire-type EGC pulled in.
MC armor relied on as the only ground where the cable is not listed for it.
Wire-type EGC run outside the raceway instead of with the circuit conductors.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the EMT is the ground, so the green wire is optional — and a flex whip is the same thing.' Wrong twice. Flex only counts within its limits — 6 ft combined in the ground-return path, listed fittings, and the overcurrent limits of the section. Past those limits the flex is just a raceway, and a wire-type EGC must be pulled with the circuit.

page_quiz.question: What is the maximum combined length of flexible conduit allowed in the ground-return path?
page_quiz.explain_plain: FMC and LFMC count as the EGC only within the section's limits — 6 ft combined in the ground-return path, with listed fittings.

choices: Its fittings are listed and made up tight
A green wire is also pulled
page_quiz.explain_plain: The raceway itself is the path, so the joints carry the fault — fittings must be listed and tight.
