choices: Copper wire run with the circuit
A raceway method not listed in the section
Type AC armor with bonding strip
page_quiz.explain_plain: If the method is not on the 250.118 list, it is not a ground path, however solid it looks.

sections.title: Identifying the equipment grounding conductor
sections.plain_explanation:
An equipment grounding conductor is identified by its color: continuous green, green with one or more yellow stripes, or bare. The reservation runs in both directions: a white or gray conductor is never an equipment ground, a green conductor is never used as a current-carrying conductor, and a green conductor may not be re-marked into something else at the ends.
• 6 AWG and smaller: the conductor itself must be green, green with a yellow stripe, or bare for its full length. In a multiconductor cable, an insulated conductor may be re-identified as the equipment grounding conductor at each end and at every accessible point only where maintenance and supervision ensure that only qualified persons service the installation (250.119(B)).
• 4 AWG and larger (250.119(A)): an insulated conductor of another color may be identified as the equipment grounding conductor by green marking at each termination and at every point where the conductor is accessible.
sections.on_the_job: In a pull, if the green is missing, the pull is wrong — stop and fix the wire order rather than planning to tape a black conductor green at both ends of a 12 AWG run. Tape-marking is the large-conductor allowance, not a small-wire shortcut.
sections.figure_idea: Conductor lineup: green, green with yellow stripe, and bare marked as approved EGC identification; a black 12 AWG with green tape crossed out; the same tape marking at 4/0 by the lug marked approved.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The equipment grounding conductor does its whole job on the worst day of the circuit's life: a fault to a metal frame. If the green was re-marked as a hot, or a white got landed as the ground, the fault path is broken or a grounded conductor is carrying load current, and the breaker never sees the fault it was supposed to clear. The color is how the next person in the box knows the path is real.
inspection_fails: Black 12 AWG taped green at both ends and run as the equipment grounding conductor.
Green conductor re-marked with black tape and used as a hot.
White conductor landed on the ground bar as the equipment grounding conductor.
4/0 equipment ground marked green at the lugs but left unmarked at an accessible splice point.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'green tape fixes anything.' Tape marking is the allowance for conductors 4 AWG and larger (250.119(A)). On 6 AWG and smaller, the insulation itself must be green, green with a yellow stripe, or bare for the full length — a taped black 12 AWG is a violation, not a shortcut.

rows: Green, green with yellow stripe, or bare — full length

figures.alt: Lineup of conductors: green, green with a yellow stripe, and bare marked OK as equipment grounding conductors; a black 12 AWG with green tape crossed out; a 4/0 conductor with green marking at the lug marked OK.
figures.caption: Tape is the big-conductor allowance — small wire must be green for its whole length.

page_quiz.question: Which of these is a permitted identification for an equipment grounding conductor?
choices: Green with one or more yellow stripes
Black with green tape, any size
page_quiz.explain_plain: Continuous green, green with yellow stripes, or bare — those are the identifications 250.119 reserves.

page_quiz.question: A black 12 AWG conductor taped green at both ends is used as the equipment grounding conductor. Permitted?
choices: Yes — tape is allowed at the ends
No — 6 AWG and smaller must be green or bare for the full length
page_quiz.explain_plain: Tape marking is the 4 AWG-and-larger allowance in 250.119(A). Small conductors carry the color in the insulation itself.

page_quiz.question: For conductors 4 AWG and larger, an insulated conductor of another color may serve as the equipment grounding conductor if it is:
choices: Painted green for its full length
Marked green at each termination and at every accessible point
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.119(A): green marking at each termination and at every point where the conductor is accessible.

sections.title: Sizing the equipment grounding conductor
sections.plain_explanation: The green or bare conductor that runs with a circuit is sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of it — not by the size of the current-carrying conductors. The one adjustment: when circuit conductors are upsized, the equipment grounding conductor is upsized in the same proportion (250.122(B)). The EGC must carry fault current back to the source for as long as the breaker takes to open, which is why a long, upsized run with a standard ground is a defect even though every receptacle tests 'grounded.' The table below runs to 1200A; it continues to 6000A for large commercial work. Where one equipment ground serves several circuits in a raceway, it is sized for the largest overcurrent device among them.
sections.on_the_job: When you upsize a run for voltage drop, upsize the ground in the same proportion and write both sizes on the plan. Cable assemblies do this for you; conduit runs do not — check the pull list. Worked example: a 20A circuit is upsized from 12 AWG to 8 AWG for a long run, and the ground grows by the same proportion — 12 AWG to 8 AWG — not the 12 AWG the table alone would give a 20A circuit. On a commercial job, that upsized ground goes on the pull list next to the upsized conductors, or it does not get pulled.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: on a CCA branch run, the equipment grounding conductor and its connectors still have to be suitable for the installation — check AL-CU markings where CCA is involved.
sections.figure_idea: A conduit pull list showing a circuit upsized from 12 to 10 AWG for a long run, with the equipment ground upsized beside it.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: On a ground fault, the EGC is the path that lets the breaker see a large current and trip fast. An undersized ground chokes that path: fault current falls, tripping slows or never happens, and the metal case of the faulted equipment sits energized, waiting for a hand. Sizing the ground to the breaker ahead of it matches it to the fault current that breaker can pass.
inspection_fails: Conductors upsized for voltage drop, equipment ground left at table size — 250.122(B) requires the same proportion.
One ground in a shared raceway sized for the smallest circuit instead of the largest breaker ahead of it.
14 AWG ground pulled on a 30A circuit — Table 250.122 requires 10 AWG copper.
CCA branch run with EGC connectors not marked AL-CU (S-10).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the ground off the conductor size on the pull list. A 100A feeder pulled in oversized conductors still takes the 8 AWG copper ground Table 250.122 assigns to a 100A device. The reverse also fails: conductors upsized for voltage drop with a table-size ground left behind — 250.122(B) grows the ground in the same proportion.

tables.caption: Table 250.122 — equipment grounding conductor (NEC 2020)
tables.note: Table continues to 6000A. Upsized circuit conductors: increase the EGC in the same proportion — 250.122(B).

The rating of the overcurrent device ahead of it

page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.122(B) increases the equipment grounding conductor proportionally whenever the circuit conductors are upsized.

sections.title: Frames of ranges and dryers on existing circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
New work is 4-wire: the frames of ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers, and the outlet or junction boxes on their circuits connect to the equipment grounding conductor. This section keeps the older 3-wire arrangement lawful only for an existing branch circuit where no equipment grounding conductor is present in the outlet or junction box, and only if all four conditions are met:
• The supply is 120/240-volt, single-phase, 3-wire, or 208Y/120-volt from a 3-phase, 4-wire wye system.
• The grounded conductor is not smaller than 10 AWG copper or 8 AWG aluminum.
• That conductor is insulated, or uninsulated only as part of a Type SE cable on a circuit originating at the service equipment.
• The grounding contacts of receptacles furnished as part of the equipment are bonded to the equipment.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call, identify what is actually in the wall before quoting a receptacle swap. If the circuit is being replaced or extended as new work, pull 4-wire and set a 4-wire receptacle and cord; never create a new 3-wire installation, and never leave the strap in place on a 4-wire hookup. On a dryer swap in an older Kissimmee home, check the box first: a 3-wire SE run from the service panel, with a 10 AWG copper neutral and the receptacle's grounding contacts bonded to the frame, meets all four conditions, so the existing circuit may stay. The same run from a subpanel with a bare SE neutral fails the third condition — that is a rewire conversation, not a receptacle swap.
sections.figure_idea: A dryer back panel showing the bonding strap removed and a 4-wire cord's green lead landed on the frame screw.

nec2023_change.change: Old 3-wire range and dryer circuits fed with service-entrance (SE) cable from a panel that isn't the service can keep using the neutral for the frame, once the bare neutral is covered. New 250.140(B)(5): existing SE cable from equipment other than the service can bond the frame through its neutral, if that neutral is insulated or covered.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 250.140 Existing range and dryer circuits

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 250.140: Old 3-wire range and dryer circuits fed with service-entrance (SE) cable from a panel that isn't the service can keep using the neutral for the frame, once the bare neutral is covered. New 250.140(B)(5): existing SE cable from equipment other than the service can bond the frame through its neutral, if that neutral is insulated or covered.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: On a 3-wire hookup the frame is bonded to the neutral, so the metal case of the dryer sits at neutral potential. If that neutral ever opens or goes high-resistance, the frame can rise toward line voltage through the heating element — and the person touching the dryer and a faucet at the same time becomes the path. Four-wire wiring gives the frame its own grounding conductor, so a fault trips the breaker instead of energizing the case.
inspection_fails: Bonding strap left in place on a 4-wire dryer or range hookup — the frame is still tied to the neutral.
New 3-wire receptacle and cord installed on a remodel circuit.
3-wire arrangement kept on a circuit fed from a subpanel with an uninsulated SE neutral — fails the originating-at-service condition.
Grounded conductor smaller than 10 AWG copper (or 8 AWG aluminum) on a kept 3-wire circuit.
Range or dryer frame not connected to the equipment grounding conductor on new 4-wire work.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that 3-wire range and dryer circuits are simply 'grandfathered.' They are not: 250.140 allows the arrangement only on an existing circuit, with no equipment grounding conductor in the box, and all four conditions met. The second trap is leaving the bonding strap in place when a 4-wire cord goes on — the strap ties the frame back to the neutral and defeats the new grounding conductor.

tables.caption: The four conditions for keeping a 3-wire hookup (250.140)
rows: Supply is 120/240 V single-phase 3-wire, or 208Y/120 V from a wye system
Grounded conductor not smaller than 10 AWG copper or 8 AWG aluminum
Conductor insulated, or bare only in Type SE cable from the service equipment
Receptacle grounding contacts furnished with the equipment bonded to the equipment

figures.alt: Back of a clothes dryer wired with a 4-wire cord: the bonding strap is removed and the green grounding lead lands on the frame screw, beside panels contrasting the existing-only 3-wire arrangement and the neutral minimum sizes.
figures.caption: The 4-wire hookup: strap out, green lead on the frame screw.

page_quiz.question: A 4-wire cord is installed on a dryer. What happens to the bonding strap?
choices: Leave it — it does no harm
Remove it; the frame bonds through the green conductor
Move it to the neutral terminal
page_quiz.explain_plain: With a 4-wire cord the frame connects to the equipment grounding conductor. A strap left in place ties the frame back to the neutral.

page_quiz.question: What is the smallest grounded conductor allowed on a kept 3-wire range circuit?
page_quiz.explain_plain: One of the four conditions: the grounded conductor must not be smaller than 10 AWG copper or 8 AWG aluminum.

page_quiz.question: A 3-wire dryer circuit may stay in service only when…
choices: It is an existing circuit, no grounding conductor is in the box, and all four conditions are met
The dryer is less than 10 years old
page_quiz.explain_plain: 250.140 is an existing-circuit permission with four conditions — it never authorizes a new 3-wire installation.
